passages.title: The Book from the Forgiver and Severe Punisher
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the surah's opening statement of who is speaking in the Qur'an. The first three name the Sender by a cluster of His attributes — mighty, all-knowing, forgiver of sin, acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment, the Bestower — and close with the return of everything to Him. The next three turn to the people who dispute His signs, and warn that their present prosperity settles nothing. Ibn Kathir gives the thread that ties it together when he explains why mercy and punishment are named in the same breath: these two attributes are often mentioned together in the Qur'an so that people will remain in a state of both hope and fear.

## Ḥā Mīm — the surahs they called "the brides"

Surah 40 begins a run of seven surahs, from here to Surah al-Aḥqāf (46), each opening with the two letters **ḥā mīm**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they are known collectively as *al-Ḥawāmīm* (or *āl Ḥā Mīm*, "the family of Ḥā Mīm"), and records the early praise given to them. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) called them *dībāj al-Qurʼān* — *dībāj*, in Arabic, being the cloth of pure silk, and here signifying embellishment. Misʿar ibn Kidām said, "They used to be called *al-ʿarāʼis* — the brides." And Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Everything has an essence, and the essence of the Qur'an is the family of Ḥā Mīm." Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān trace these reports to *Faḍāʼil al-Qurʼān* of the great scholar Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām.

Ibn Kathir also records a parable of Ibn Masʿūd's, narrated by Ḥumayd ibn Zanjuyah and recorded by al-Baghawī: a man sets out to find a place for his family to stay. He comes upon land showing the evidence of rainfall, and while he is walking about admiring it he suddenly comes upon beautiful gardens. He says, "I liked the first traces of rainfall, but this is far better." It was said to him: the first place is like the Qur'an, and these beautiful gardens are like the splendour of the family of Ḥā Mīm in relation to the rest of the Qur'an. And Ibn Masʿūd said, "When I reach the family of Ḥā Mīm, it is like reaching a beautiful garden, so I take my time."

**What do the letters mean?** Ibn Kathir declines to repeat the discussion here, referring the reader back to his treatment of the individual letters at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some commentators held *Ḥā Mīm* to be a name of Allah, but adds that in the sight of the early authorities the *ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt* — the isolated letters — are all from the category of *mutashābihāt*, those of hidden meaning: their meanings known to Allah alone, or a secret between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.

**Ḥā Mīm in battle.** Ibn Kathir records a hadith from Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī, from one who heard it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: *"When you go to bed tonight, recite Ḥā Mīm, lā yunṣarūn."* Ibn Kathir states that its chain of narrators is *ṣaḥīḥ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same report by way of Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufrah (may Allah be pleased with him) — a narration in Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī through a chain rated *ṣaḥīḥ* — with the setting of a night watch during a military expedition, and the wording that should you be attacked at night, you recite *Ḥā Mīm lā yunṣarūn*, praying thereby that the enemy does not succeed. Maʿārif notes some narrations carry the variant *Ḥā Mīm lā yunṣarū*, and draws the lesson that *Ḥā Mīm* serves as a fortress against the enemy.

There is a second report, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Ibn Kathir: al-Bazzār, quoting his own chains of authority in his *Musnad*, reports from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever recites Āyat al-Kursī and the first three verses of Surah al-Muʼmin — up to *ilayhi'l-maṣīr* — early in the day will remain safe that day from everything bad and painful. Maʿārif is careful to add that at-Tirmidhī also reports it, though one of the links in the chain of authority is doubtful. That honesty is part of the report, and worth passing on with it.

## The Book, and the Lord it comes from

*Tanzīl al-kitāb min Allāhi'l-ʿAzīzi'l-ʿAlīm* — "The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Knower." Ibn Kathir explains: this book, the Qur'an, is from Allah, **the Owner of might and knowledge, who cannot be overtaken and from whom nothing is hidden, not even an ant concealed beneath many layers.**

The next ayah then pours out four descriptions of that same Lord in a row, and each one repays slowing down over.

**Ghāfir al-dhanb — Forgiver of sin.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazharī, opens the root: the word literally means the one who puts a cover on sins, in the sense that they are no longer seen or known by anyone.

**Qābil al-tawb — Acceptor of repentance.** Why two phrases when the sense of both seems almost the same? Mazharī's answer, as Maʿārif reports it, is precise: saying *ghāfir al-dhanb* indicates that Allah already possesses the standing authority and power to forgive a servant's sin **even without repentance**, while forgiving those who do repent is yet another attribute of Allah. Ibn Kathir reads the pair along the axis of time: **He forgives sins that have been committed in the past, and He accepts repentance for sins that may be committed in the future** — from the one who repents and submits to Him.

**Shadīd al-ʿiqāb — Severe in punishment.** Ibn Kathir specifies whom this concerns: the one who **persists in transgression and prefers the life of this world, who stubbornly turns away from the commands of Allah and commits sin.** And he explains why mercy and punishment sit side by side, quoting: *"Declare unto My servants that truly I am the Oft-Forgiving, the Most-Merciful. And that My torment is indeed the most painful torment"* (15:49–50). These two attributes, he says, are often mentioned together in the Qur'an **so that people will remain in a state of both hope and fear**.

**Dhi'ṭ-ṭawl — the Bestower.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (Mazharī) gives the root sense of *ṭawl* as vastness and being free of need, adding that it could also mean power or favour. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said it means **"He is Generous and Rich — Independent of means."** Ibn Kathir draws it out: He is Most Generous to His servants, granting ongoing blessings for which they can never sufficiently thank Him — *"And if you would count the favours of Allah, never could you be able to count them"* (16:18).

Then the ayah closes: **Lā ilāha illā Huwa.** Ibn Kathir: there is **none that is equal to Him in all His attributes**; there is no god or lord besides Him. And **ilayhi'l-maṣīr** — to Him is the final return: all things will come back to Him, and He will reward or punish each person according to his deeds. Ibn Kathir pairs this with *"and He is Swift at reckoning"* (13:41).

## The same names, turned into prayer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Ibn Kathir) relates a strange event told by Thābit al-Bunānī. He was with Muṣʿab ibn az-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) in a certain section of the city of Kufa, and walked into a garden to pray two rakʿahs. Before beginning, he recited 40:1–3. Suddenly he saw a man in Yemeni attire, astride a white mule, standing behind him. The man said: when you say *ghāfir al-dhanb*, pray with it *"yā ghāfira'dh-dhanbi'ghfir lī"* — O Forgiver of sins, forgive me. When you say *qābil al-tawb*, pray *"yā qābila't-tawbi'qbal tawbatī"* — O Accepter of repentance, accept my repentance. When you say *shadīd al-ʿiqāb*, pray *"yā shadīda'l-ʿiqābi lā tuʿāqibnī"* — O Allah, severe in punishment, please do not punish me. And when you say *dhi'ṭ-ṭawl*, pray *"yā dha'ṭ-ṭawli ṭul ʿalayya bi-khayr"* — O source of power, bestow the best upon me.

Thābit says that after hearing this, when he looked back there was no one there; he went to the gate of the garden and asked the people there whether they had seen a man in Yemeni attire pass through, and everyone said they had not. In another narration from Thābit it is added that people think this person was Ilyās (peace be upon him), while the other narration does not mention it — and Maʿārif reports it just so, without pressing the claim. The narration itself calls what he was given good counsel, and the practice is immediately usable: when one of these names passes your lips in recitation, answer it with the request that name invites.

**A letter that brought a man back.** Ibn Kathir reports, on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that among the Syrians who used to visit ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) was a man of strong and dignified bearing. When he did not show up for longer than usual, ʿUmar asked after him. People said, "O Commander of the Believers, please do not ask about him — he has become a drunkard."

ʿUmar called his scribe and dictated a letter: *"From ʿUmar son of al-Khaṭṭāb to so-and-so son of so-and-so. Peace be upon you. After that, I praise Allah before you, other than whom there is no god worthy of worship. He is the One who forgives sins and accepts repentance, the One who is severe in punishment, the One who is the source of all power. There is no god but He. To Him is the ultimate return."* Then he turned to those around him and said, "Let us all join in to pray for him, that Allah reverses his heart and accepts his repentance." He instructed the messenger not to hand the letter to anyone but the man himself, and not until he had become sober.

When the man received it he read it repeatedly and thoughtfully, realising that it carried a warning of punishment against him with a concurrent promise of forgiveness for him. Then he started weeping. He stopped drinking, and made such a firm *tawbah* that he never touched it again.

When ʿUmar learnt what those words had done, he said to the people around him: **in such matters you too should do the same. When some brother falls into a slip of conduct, think of ways to bring him back to his normal and better self. Prompt him to turn to Allah, to place his trust in Him, to rely on His mercy. Pray to Allah for him, that he be enabled to repent. And do not become an accomplice of Shayṭān against him** — for if you chide him or infuriate him and thereby estrange him from his religion, you would actually be helping Shayṭān.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out as guidance for anyone who works for the betterment of Allah's creation and serves in the field of *tablīgh* and *daʿwah*: first pray for the person yourself, then use soft ways to bring him towards that betterment. Do not be aggressive towards him, for it would do him no good; in fact it would amount to helping Shayṭān, who would push him onto more ways of error.

## Those who dispute the signs — and what their prosperity proves

Ibn Kathir reads *"None disputes the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve"* as a statement about what happens **after clear proof has come**: no one then rejects or disputes His signs except those who disbelieve — those who reject the signs of Allah and His proof and evidence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this ayah declares quarrelling over the Qur'an an act of *kufr*, and cites the words of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Surely, quarrelling (jidāl) in the Qur'an is kufr"* — reported by al-Baghawī and al-Bayhaqī in *ash-Shuʿab* from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), and reported by Abū Dāwūd and al-Ḥākim, who rated it *ṣaḥīḥ*. It also records that it appears in Hadith that the Prophet ﷺ one day heard two persons quarrelling about a verse of the Qur'an; he became angry and came out with his blessed face showing the signs of anger, and said that communities before them were ruined because they had started quarrelling in the matter of the Book of Allah — reported by Muslim from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb.

**A sincere student could be frightened off study by that, so the scholars define the term carefully.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī, al-Qurṭubī and Mazharī, says the *jidāl* declared *kufr* means throwing taunts, passing sarcastic remarks, engineering disputes over self-invented and absurd doubts, or giving a verse a meaning that runs counter to other verses of the Qur'an and to the binding textual imperatives of the Sunnah — something that amounts to alteration of the Qur'an. Otherwise, honest inquiry about something ambiguous or vague, trying to find the solution of a difficult word or expression, or mutually investigating and discussing possibilities while deducing rulings from a verse are **not** included under this *jidāl*; in fact, they say, it is an act of *thawāb*, reward, in its own place.

Then: *"So let not their going about through the land deceive you."* Ibn Kathir explains this movement as their wealth and luxurious life, and pairs it with *"Let not the free disposal of the disbelievers throughout the land deceive you. A brief enjoyment; then their ultimate abode is Hell — and worst indeed is that place of rest"* (3:196–197), and *"We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to enter a great torment"* (31:24).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the concrete Makkan picture. The disbelievers of Quraysh used to travel with their trading caravans to Yemen in winter and to Syria in summer. Because of their services to the Baytullāh at Makkah they were held in esteem all over Arabia, so they remained safe during their travels and profited from their commercial ventures; this was the backbone of their wealth and territorial power. That all this continued despite the challenge of Islam and of the Prophet ﷺ was a matter of pride for them — *"Had we been the culprits in the sight of Allah, all these blessings would have been taken away from us."* This situation, Maʿārif observes, **could have made even some Muslims easy victims of doubt**. So the ayah answers it: Allah had granted them a temporary respite, in His wisdom and under His expedient consideration — so let Muslims not be deceived by the leash given to them. Once the respite is over, punishment will visit them and this territorial power will be taken away. It started from the Battle of Badr, and up to the Conquest of Makkah it manifested itself fully and conclusively within a span of six years.

## Nations that were seized before them

Ibn Kathir says that here **Allah consoles His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ** for the rejection of his people, telling him that he has an example in the Prophets who came before him — peace and blessings be upon them all — for their nations disbelieved them and opposed them, and only a few believed in them.

The history is compressed into a single ayah. *The people of Nūḥ denied before them* — and Ibn Kathir notes that Nūḥ was the first Messenger whom Allah sent to denounce and forbid idol worship. *And the groups after them* — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, from every nation. *And every nation plotted against their Messenger to seize him* — they wanted to kill him by any means possible, and **some of them did kill their Messenger**. *And they disputed by means of falsehood, to refute the truth with it* — they came up with specious arguments with which to dispute a truth that was plain and clear. Then the pattern breaks: *So I seized them* — "I destroyed them," Ibn Kathir explains, "because of the sins they committed." *And how was My punishment!* — meaning: you have heard how severe and painful My punishment and vengeance was. Qatādah's comment is a single stunned line: **"It was terrible, by Allah."**

And so the closing ayah: *Thus has the Word of your Lord been justified against those who disbelieved, that they will be the dwellers of the Fire.* Ibn Kathir: just as the Word of punishment was justified against those of the past nations who disbelieved, so too is it justified against these disbelievers who have rejected you and gone against you, O Muhammad ﷺ — **and it is even more justified against them, because if they have disbelieved in you, there is no certainty that they will believe in any other Prophet.** And Allah knows best.

That returns the passage to where it began. The Book comes from the Owner of might and knowledge, who forgives what is past and accepts repentance for what may come, and who is severe with the one who persists and turns stubbornly away — the two named together, as Ibn Kathir says, so that people remain in both hope and fear. The disputers outside are not new, and their prosperity is only a respite. And for anyone who wants the other side of that balance, the passage even hands over the words: *yā ghāfira'dh-dhanbi'ghfir lī* — O Forgiver of sins, forgive me.

passages.title: Angels of the Throne pray for the believers
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat lift the curtain on the highest creation in the universe and show us what they are doing: the angels who carry the Throne of Allah, and the ranks of angels gathered around it, are praising their Lord — and praying for you. What holds the passage together is a single unbroken sentence: ayah 7 introduces these angels and begins their supplication, and ayat 8 and 9 are the rest of that same supplication, word for word, until it closes on "and that is the supreme success."

Read it that way and something remarkable emerges. The Qur'an does not merely tell us the angels pray for the believers; it lets us overhear the prayer itself.

## Who these angels are

Ibn Kathir describes them as "the angels who are close to Him, the bearers of the Throne, and the angels who are around Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds detail: the bearers of the Throne are at present four, and on the Day of Qiyamah they will be eight; as for the angels around the Throne, only Allah knows their number, and Maʿārif notes that some hadith narrations give the number of their rows as reaching several hundred thousand. Maʿārif also gives their traditional name — *karrūbī*, which it sets alongside the English "cherubim" — and describes them as angels close to Allah.

Shahr bin Hawshab said that the bearers of the Throne are eight: four of them say, *Glory and praise be to You, O Allah; to You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge.* And four of them say: *Glory and praise be to You, O Allah; to You be praise for Your forgiveness after Your power.* Look at what those two phrases mean. Allah knows exactly what we have done — and still He is forbearing. Allah has complete power to seize us — and still He forgives. The angels closest to the Throne have made the very restraint of Allah their theme of praise. And it is precisely from that theme that their prayer for sinful human beings flows: Shahr bin Hawshab's report moves straight from those two praises to what these angels say when they pray for forgiveness for the believers.

## What they do before they ask

Ayah 7 gives their state in three verbs before a single request is made.

**They glorify with praise** — *yusabbiḥūna bi-ḥamdi rabbihim*. Ibn Kathir notes that the two are combined: *tasbīḥ* (glorification) implies that Allah is free of any shortcomings, while *ḥamd* (praise) is an affirmation of praise. One clears away everything unworthy of Him; the other affirms what is worthy of Him.

**They believe in Him** — *wa yu'minūna bihi*. Even of angels who are, in Ibn Kathir's words, "close to Him," the ayah says that they believe. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning "they humbly submit themselves before Him." Faith at that station is not the acquiring of information; it is submission.

**And they ask forgiveness for those who believe** — *wa yastaghfirūna lilladhīna āmanū*. Ibn Kathir specifies who is meant: "those among the people of earth who believe in the Unseen." That contrast is the heart of the passage. Angels at the Throne are pleading on behalf of people who have seen none of it — who believe in the Unseen, on the strength of a message, in a world full of reasons to doubt. The nearest creation intercedes for the most veiled.

## Prayed for behind your back

Ibn Kathir draws a conclusion that turns this passage from awe into intimacy: **Allah commanded His angels who are close to Him to pray for the believers in their absence** — and so it is part of the very nature of angels that they say *Amin* when a believer prays for his brother in his absence. He cites Sahih Muslim:

> "When a Muslim prays for his brother in his absence, the angel says, 'Amin, and may you have something similar to it.'"

Notice how the two halves fit. Above, angels are praying for people they have never met. Below, when you pray for a Muslim who is not in the room — someone who will never know you did it, who cannot thank you, from whom you gain nothing — you are doing on earth what Ibn Kathir says the angels close to Allah were commanded to do. And the angel's response is not merely "Amin"; it is "and may you have something similar to it." The supplication you send away comes back to you carrying its own reward.

Mutarrif bin ʿAbdullah bin Ash-Shikhkhīr drew the plainest lesson from these ayat: **"The most sincere of the servants of Allah towards the believers are the angels."** He then recited the words *"Our Lord! And make them enter the ʿAdn (Eternal) Paradises which You have promised them,"* and afterwards added the counterpart: "The most treacherous of the servants of Allah towards the believers are the Shayāṭīn." Two unseen parties surround the believer. One wishes him ruin; the other wishes him Paradise and asks for it by name. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the scholars' two ways of accounting for the angels' devotion: either Allah has appointed them to this task, or their nature is such that they keep praying for the good servants of Allah.

## The prayer itself: how the angels ask (ayah 7)

The supplication is a masterclass in how to approach Allah, and its order is deliberate.

**They begin with Allah, not with the request.** *"Our Lord! You comprehend all things in mercy and knowledge."* Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "Your mercy encompasses their sins and Your knowledge encompasses all their deeds, words and action." They do not hide the human record — they place it inside something larger. The sins are real; the mercy encompasses them. And observe the order in the ayah itself: mercy is named before knowledge.

**Then they name who they are asking for.** *"So forgive those who repent and follow Your way."* Ibn Kathir explains: "forgive the sinners when they repent to You and turn to You and give up their former ways, following Your commands to do good and abstain from evil." Two things, and they belong together — repentance is the turning back, and following His way is what the turning looks like in practice. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says these angels pray for all believers, and particularly for those who repent from their sins and follow the Sharīʿah of the Holy Prophet ﷺ.

**Then the first request: rescue.** *"And save them from the torment of the blazing Fire."* Ibn Kathir's rendering is physical and urgent — "snatch them away from the punishment of Hell, which is a painful, agonizing punishment." Not "keep them at a distance," but a seizing and pulling away.

## Ayah 8: the prayer widens to include your family

Having asked for rescue, the angels ask for arrival — and then they ask for something no one thinks to ask for themselves.

*"Our Lord! And make them enter the ʿAdn (Eternal) Gardens which You have promised them."* They ask Allah for what He has already promised — taking hold of a promise and asking to see it fulfilled.

Then: *"and to the righteous among their fathers, their wives, and their offspring."* Ibn Kathir explains the purpose: "bring them together so that they may find delight in one another in neighboring dwellings." Paradise is not conceived here as isolated bliss. Part of the reward is the people you love, nearby.

But there is an obvious problem, and the Qur'an answers it. Family members do not all reach the same rank. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel ayah: *"And those who believe and whose offspring follow them in faith — to them shall We join their offspring, and We shall not decrease the reward of their deeds in anything"* (52:21). His comment: "all of them will be made equal in status. In this way they may delight in one another's company; the one who is in the higher status will not lose anything. On the contrary We will raise the one whose deeds are of a lower status so that they will become equal, as a favor and a blessing from Us." No one is demoted so the family can be together; the lower is lifted. And the lifting is explicitly named as a favor and a blessing.

Saʿīd bin Jubayr gave this a scene. When the believer enters Paradise, he will ask where his father, son and brother are. It will be said to him: they did not reach the same level of good deeds as you did. He will say: *but I did it for my sake and for theirs.* Then they will be brought to join him in that higher degree. Ibn Kathir reports it, and Saʿīd bin Jubayr then recited this very ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a scholarly note worth pausing on. This report is *mawqūf* — which Maʿārif explains as a tradition from a Companion who does not connect it to the Holy Prophet ﷺ. Having reported the narration in Tafsīr Mazharī, its author said that it has the same authority and force as a *marfūʿ* report — a tradition attributed to the Holy Prophet ﷺ — and that it is explicit on the point that the "doing good" held as a precondition for this privilege means īmān, adhering to the true faith.

**Who qualifies as "the righteous among them"?** This is the crucial limit, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise about it: those meant are the ones who meet the criterion of goodness that makes them deserving of forgiveness — a criterion requiring that **they departed from this world adhering to their īmān**. Maʿārif draws the conclusion directly: īmān, faith, is the basic condition of salvation (*najāh*); after īmān come the other good deeds. So the mercy is vast — such is the munificence of Allah, Maʿārif says, that relatives of lesser rank are let in alongside their people so that their happiness becomes total and complete — but it is not indiscriminate. Faith is the thread the whole family is pulled up by.

**"Verily, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise."** The angels close this request with two of Allah's names, and both are chosen for the job. Ibn Kathir on *al-ʿAzīz*: "the One Whom none can resist or overwhelm; what You will happens and what You do not will does not happen." On *al-Ḥakīm*: "Wise in all that You say and do, in all that You legislate and decree." Together they mean: nothing can block this gathering-together if You will it, and nothing about it will be out of place if You decree it.

## Ayah 9: saved from sins, and from what sins do

The final request is short and, at first glance, a repetition — but it is not. *"And save them from the sins."* Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning **the actions and the consequences**. Two protections in one word: keep them from the deeds, and keep them from what those deeds bring.

*"And whomsoever You save from the sins that Day"* — Ibn Kathir identifies "that Day" as the Day of Resurrection. This is the moment the whole prayer has been aiming at.

*"Him verily, You have taken into mercy"* — that is, Ibn Kathir says, "You have protected him and saved him from punishment." Notice what mercy is glossed as here: on that Day, being taken into mercy is being protected and spared.

*"And that is the supreme success"* — *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm*. The angels' prayer has asked for forgiveness, rescue from the Fire, admission to the Gardens of ʿAdn, and the gathering of believing family. Nothing else in the passage is called success. That is.

## Living it

**Pray for people behind their backs.** Ibn Kathir says Allah commanded the angels close to Him to pray for the believers in their absence, and the report in Sahih Muslim adds that the angel answers *Amin* — and asks the same for you. Absent friends, the sick, the struggling, the dead: name them when they are not there to hear it.

**Repent, and then follow the way.** The angels' prayer is worded around *those who repent and follow Your way*, and Maʿārif notes they pray particularly for those who repent from their sins and follow the Sharīʿah of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. To be inside that supplication is not automatic; turning back to Allah and holding to what He commanded is the door.

**Work for your family's faith, not only their comfort.** The angels ask for the believer's parents, spouses, and children. Saʿīd bin Jubayr's believer says, "I did it for my sake and for theirs." But Maʿārif's condition stands: what qualifies a relative is that they left this world adhering to their īmān. That is the one thing worth spending yourself on for the people in your house.

**Take courage from who is on your side.** As Mutarrif said, of all Allah's servants the angels are the foremost among those who wish well for believers. Whatever the day looked like, at the highest point in creation there are beings praising Allah's forbearance after His knowledge and His forgiveness after His power, and asking Him to forgive you and to bring your family in with you.

passages.title: The disbelievers' plea and Allah's contempt
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single courtroom scene set after the verdict. In ayah 10 a voice calls out to the disbelievers in the Fire; in ayah 11 they answer with a carefully argued plea for a second chance; in ayah 12 that plea is answered — not with a "no" so much as with a diagnosis of why the answer is no. What holds the passage together is one idea: regret arriving too late, and a self-hatred that turns out to be smaller than the reality it is reacting to.

## "It will be announced to them" — ayah 10

The announcement is made *to* them, and the ayah does not name who makes it. Ibn Kathir fills that in. He places the scene precisely: this is the moment the disbelievers have entered Hell and sunk into the agonising depth of the fire, and **the angels will tell them, in a loud voice**, what they are told here.

And what are they told? The key word is **maqt** — rendered in the translation as "contempt", and by Ibn Kathir as "aversion" and as "hatred". The ayah says: *Allah's maqt* was **greater** — *akbar* — *than your maqt of yourselves.*

Ibn Kathir explains the comparison by first explaining their side of it. When they actually experience the unbearable punishment of Allah, **they will hate themselves with the utmost hatred** — not a vague self-pity, but hatred *because of the sins they committed in the past, which were the cause of their entering the Fire*. There is no one left to blame. The self-hatred of a person who knows precisely what he did and precisely what it cost him is about as intense a hatred as a creature can hold.

And that, says the ayah, is the *smaller* of the two.

## When Allah's contempt was — and why that matters

Read the second half of ayah 10 carefully: *"when you were called to the Faith but you used to refuse."* The maqt being spoken of is not something that began in Hell. Ibn Kathir is explicit: it is Allah's hatred towards them **in this world**, when faith was offered to them and they rejected it — and *that* is greater than their hatred towards themselves in the situation they are now in.

That is exactly how Qatadah read it. Ibn Kathir quotes him: "Allah's hatred for the people of misguidance — when Faith is presented to them in this world, and they turn away from it and refuse to accept it — is greater than their hatred for themselves when they see the punishment of Allah with their own eyes on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also the view of **al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, as-Suddi, Dharr bin 'Ubaydullah al-Hamdani, 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, and Ibn Jarir at-Tabari**, may Allah have mercy on them all. That is a striking unanimity among the early commentators, and it locates the whole force of the ayah.

So the announcement is really this: *the day you were turning down the invitation to faith — thinking nothing much of it, feeling nothing much about it — the estimate of what you were doing was already more severe than the estimate you have finally arrived at now, in the Fire, with your own eyes open.* Their present agony has not caught up to the truth. It is still short of it.

## "You made us die twice and gave us life twice" — ayah 11

Ibn Kathir observes something easy to miss: compared with the pleas of the damned recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an, **here they speak more eloquently**. They do not simply beg. They introduce their plea — they build an argument first, and only then make the request.

The argument is a theological one. **Ath-Thawri narrated from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Ibn Mas'ud** (may Allah be pleased with him) that this ayah is like the ayah: *"How can you disbelieve in Allah? Seeing that you were dead and He gave you life. Then He will give you death, then again will bring you to life and then unto Him you will return"* (2:28). The two deaths and the two lives are the sequence that ayah lays out. Ibn Kathir reports that this was also the view of **Ibn 'Abbas, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, and Abu Malik**, and says plainly: this is undoubtedly the correct view.

Ibn Kathir renders the sense of their words as: *by Your almighty power, You have brought us to life after we were dead, then You caused us to die after we were alive; You are able to do whatever You will.* That is the whole point of their opening. They are not describing their biography for its own sake. They are establishing a premise — **You have already done this; You are able to do whatever You will** — and then, on the strength of that premise, asking.

Then the confession: *"Now we confess our sins."* Ibn Kathir: *we confess our sins and admit that we wronged ourselves in the world.* Every excuse they ever offered has been dropped. And then the request, in ayah 11's closing words: *"then is there any way to get out?"* Ibn Kathir unpacks the intent: *will You answer our prayer to send us back to the world, for You are able to do that, so that we might do deeds different from those which we used to do? Then if we go back to our former ways, we will indeed be wrongdoers.*

It is worth pausing on what has just happened. They have argued correctly about Allah's power. They have confessed accurately about their sins. They have offered exactly the terms a sincere man would offer. And it is all worth nothing, because it arrives after the door has shut.

## The escalating plea — where this scene sits

Ibn Kathir sets ayah 11 inside a sequence he traces across the Qur'an, and seeing the sequence makes the passage land harder. The plea to return gets more desperate at every stage, and is refused at every stage:

- **Standing before Allah in the arena of Resurrection**, heads hung: *"Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back, that we will do righteous good deeds. Verily, we now believe with certainty"* (32:12). Ibn Kathir: they will get no response.
- **Held over the Fire**, looking at the punishments in it, they ask even more fervently than before: *"Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord, and we would be of the believers"* (6:27). Again, no response — and Allah's own comment follows: *"But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars"* (6:28).
- **Inside it**, having tasted its heat, its hooked rods of iron and its chains, their plea is at its most desperate and fervent: *"Our Lord! Bring us out, we shall do righteous good deeds, not that we used to do."* The reply: *"Did We not give you lives long enough, so that whosoever would receive admonition could receive it? And the warner came to you. So taste you. For the wrongdoers there is no helper"* (35:37).
- And: *"Our Lord! Bring us out of this. If ever we return, then indeed we shall be wrongdoers."* He will say: *"Remain you in it with ignominy! And speak you not to Me"* (23:107–108).

Our passage belongs to that same drama, and Ibn Kathir singles it out as the version in which they speak most eloquently.

## The answer — ayah 12

Ayah 12 opens with *"This is because…"* Ibn Kathir gives the shape of the reply: first the response itself, **"There is no way for you to go back to the world,"** and then the reason for it. And the reason is not that Allah is unable, since they have just conceded He is able. The reason is what they are.

*"This is because, when Allah Alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when partners were joined to Him, you believed!"*

This is a diagnosis, and it is devastating in its precision. Their problem was never an inability to believe — they believed readily. Their belief simply ran in the wrong direction: **tawhid** — worshipping Allah alone, with no partner — was what they rejected, and **shirk** — joining partners to Him — was what they accepted. Mention Allah alone, and they disbelieved. Attach a partner to Him, and they believed.

Ibn Kathir gives the force of the sentence as: *if you were to go back, this is how you would be.* The plea in ayah 11 is answered by the character revealed in ayah 12. Send them back and the same reflex fires again — which is precisely what Allah says elsewhere of them: *"But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars"* (6:28).

Their promise is sincere in the Fire and false everywhere else. Ibn Kathir sums up their condition in the words of the reason given to them: *your nature will not accept the truth and be governed by it, you would reject it and ignore it.*

## "So the judgement is only with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great"

The passage closes not on the criminals but on the Judge. Ibn Kathir on *"So the judgement is only with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great!"*: He is **the Judge of His creation, the Just Who is never unjust**. He guides whomsoever He wills and sends astray whomsoever He wills; He has mercy on whomsoever He wills and punishes whomsoever He wills; there is no deity except Him.

That is where the scene ends — with the plea heard, the record read, and the verdict resting where it has always rested.

## Living it

The passage is not primarily about them. It is a warning laid in front of anyone still alive, and it asks two concrete things.

**Take the invitation seriously the day it arrives.** The whole weight of ayah 10, as Qatadah and the commentators after him read it, falls on a moment in *this* world — the moment faith was presented and turned away from. That moment felt like nothing at the time. Ibn Kathir's reading of the ayah says it was not nothing. Whatever call to faith or to obedience is currently in front of you is being weighed now, not later.

**Check which direction your belief runs.** Ayah 12 does not accuse them of having no religious feeling; it accuses them of having it inverted — disbelief when Allah alone was invoked, belief when partners were joined to Him. The honest question it puts to a believer is whether Allah alone, with no partner, sits easily in the heart, or whether the heart quietly prefers something added to Him.

**And confess now, while confession still counts.** Ayah 11 contains a complete confession — *we confess our sins and admit that we wronged ourselves in the world* — offered with a promise to do different deeds. Its only defect is its timing, and the answer it receives is *"There is no way for you to go back to the world."* The same words, said today, still have somewhere to go.

passages.title: Sincere worship and the Day of Meeting
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat move from the world in front of your eyes to the Day when that world is stripped away. Ayah 13 points to Allah's signs and to the rain He sends down; ayah 14 draws the one command that follows from them — call upon Allah alone, with the religion made sincerely His; and ayat 15–17 show why nothing else deserves that call: the Owner of the Throne, who sends down the revelation, is the same One before whom every person will one day stand in the open and be paid in full. The thread running through the passage is a single argument: **He alone shows, He alone provides, He alone reveals, He alone will judge — so worship Him alone.**

## The argument these ayat are answering

Ibn Kathir reads this passage as flowing straight out of the scene just before it. In ayat 10–12 the disbelievers have entered Hell. They hate themselves with the utmost hatred for the sins that brought them there, and the angels tell them in a loud voice that Allah's hatred towards them in this world — when faith was offered to them and they rejected it — is greater than the self-hatred they feel now with the punishment before their eyes. Qatadah explained the ayah exactly that way, and Ibn Kathir reports that this was also the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, Mujahid, as-Suddi, Dharr bin 'Ubaydullah al-Hamdani, 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam and Ibn Jarir at-Tabari.

Then they plead: *"Our Lord! You have made us to die twice, and You have given us life twice!"* Ibn Kathir records that ath-Thawri narrated from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that this ayah is like the ayah of Sūrah al-Baqarah, *"Seeing that you were dead and He gave you life. Then He will give you death, then again will bring you to life"* (2:28) — and this was also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and Abu Malik. Ibn Kathir says this is undoubtedly the correct view. What all of it means, he explains, is that standing before Allah in the arena of the Resurrection, the disbelievers will ask to go back. Ibn Kathir traces that plea escalating across the Qur'an — heads hung low before their Lord (32:12), then held over the Fire (6:27–28), then crying out from inside it (35:37), until the answer finally comes, *"Remain you in it with ignominy! And speak you not to Me!"* (23:107–108).

Ayah 12 gives the reason the request is refused: *"This is because, when Allah Alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when partners were joined to Him, you believed!"* Ibn Kathir's reading is chilling — the meaning, he says, is *'if you were to go back, this is how you would be,'* as in *"But if they were returned, they would certainly revert to that which they were forbidden. And indeed they are liars"* (6:28). Their nature would not accept the truth and be governed by it. Pure tawhid repelled them; shirk attracted them.

Hold that in mind, because it is exactly what ayah 14 commands the believer to be the opposite of.

## Ayah 13 — the signs everyone sees, the lesson few take

*"It is He Who shows you His Ayat and sends down provision for you from the sky."*

Ibn Kathir explains **يُرِيكُمْ آيَاتِهِ** (*yurīkum āyātihi*, "shows you His signs") as Allah demonstrating His power to His servants through the mighty signs which they see in His creation, above and below, which indicate the perfection of its Creator and Originator.

The "provision from the sky" is rain — and Ibn Kathir does not leave it as a bare fact. Through rain, crops and fruits are brought forth, and the argument is in their variety: their different colours, tastes, fragrances and forms are a sign of the Creator. It is *one kind of water*, but by His great power He makes all these things different. The sign is not merely that water falls; it is that a single input yields an endless catalogue of outputs.

Then the ayah turns, and the turn is the point: **وَمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ إِلَّا مَن يُنِيبُ** — *"And none remembers but those who turn in repentance."* Notice what it does *not* say. It does not say that only some people see the rain; everyone sees the rain. It says only some **remember**. Ibn Kathir glosses *"and none remembers"* as: no one learns a lesson or is reminded by these things, or takes them as a sign of the might of the Creator — except **مَن يُنِيبُ** (*man yunīb*), which he explains as those who have insight and turn to Allah, may He be blessed and exalted.

So the ayah does not simply say: study the evidence, and you will arrive at Allah. It ties the lesson to the one who turns to Him. Two people can stand in the same rain, and only one of them is being taught anything.

## Ayah 14 — the command, and the clause that comes with it

*"So, call you upon Allah making religion sincerely for Him, however much the disbelievers may hate."*

Everything in ayah 13 — the signs, the rain, the heart that takes the lesson — issues in this one instruction, and Ibn Kathir places it under a heading that captures its force: *the believers are commanded to worship Allah alone no matter what their circumstances.*

**ادْعُوا** (*udʿū*, "call upon") is read by Ibn Kathir in its full breadth, covering both supplication and worship: "worship Allah and call upon Him alone in all sincerity. Do not be like the idolators in conduct and beliefs." Note that both words are there — *conduct* and *beliefs*. Sincerity is not only an inward setting; it shows in how a person lives.

**مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ** (*mukhliṣīn lahu ad-dīn*) is the heart of it: the religion is to be made sincerely His — not one prayer here and there, but *ad-dīn*, the whole of it, belonging to Him with nothing skimmed off for anyone else.

Then comes the clause that keeps the command honest: **وَلَوْ كَرِهَ الْكَافِرُونَ** — *"however much the disbelievers may hate."* Sincerity does not wait for social permission. The ayah anticipates the dislike and tells you to carry on anyway.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded that after ending every prayer, 'Abdullah bin az-Zubayr used to say:

> "There is no (true) deity except Allah Alone with no partner or associate, His is the dominion and praise, for He is able to do all things; there is no strength and no power except with Allah; there is no (true) deity except Allah and we worship none but Him; to Him belongs the blessings and the virtue and good praise; there is no (true) deity except Allah, we worship Him in all sincerity even though the disbelievers may hate that."

He said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say Tahlil with this after every prayer." (*Tahlīl* means saying *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, "there is no true god except Allah.") Ibn Kathir adds that something similar was also recorded by Muslim, Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i, and that it was reported in *Ṣaḥīḥ* from Ibn az-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say it after the prescribed obligatory prayers.

Look at how it ends: **مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ وَلَوْ كَرِهَ الْكَافِرُونَ** — the words of the ayah itself, sealing the dhikr. The command of ayah 14 was not left as an abstraction. It was placed on the tongue of the believer at the close of the prayer.

## Ayah 15 — Exalted in ranks, and the Day of Meeting

*"(He is Allah) Owner of high ranks and degrees, the Owner of the Throne. He sends the revelation by His command to any of His servants He wills, that he may warn of the Day of Mutual Meeting."*

**رَفِيعُ الدَّرَجَاتِ** (*Rafīʿ ad-darajāt*) is read in more than one way, and Maarif ul Quran sets the views side by side rather than settling between them:

- Some commentators take *darajāt* to mean **attributes** — so the sense would be that His attributes of perfection are most exalted.
- **Ibn Kathir** relies on the words as they appear outwardly and says it refers to the most exalted Throne, for it comprehends all land masses and heavens and is located above them all like a roof — citing *"From Allah, the Lord of the ways of ascent. The angels and the Ruh (Jibril) ascend to Him in a Day the measure whereof is fifty thousand years"* (70:3–4).
- Others read *rafīʿ ad-darajāt* in the sense of *rāfiʿ ad-darajāt*, **the One who elevates others in ranks** — Allah raising the ranks of believers who have His fear in their hearts, as in *"We raise in ranks whom We will"* (6:83) and *"They are of various ranks with Allah"* (3:163).

On the Throne itself, Ibn Kathir reports that more than one scholar said the Throne is made of red rubies, that the width between two corners of it is the distance of a fifty-thousand-year journey, and that its height above the seventh earth is the same distance — and Maarif ul Quran notes that this measure of fifty thousand years, describing the distance from the seventh level of the earth up to the Throne, is what Ibn Kathir declares to be the preferred position of a majority of earlier and later scholars. We affirm the Throne as Allah described it, without likening it to anything created and without emptying the words of their meaning.

**يُلْقِي الرُّوحَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ** — *He sends the revelation of His command.* Here *ar-rūḥ* means revelation, as Ibn Kathir shows by pairing the ayah with *"He sends down the angels with the Ruh (revelation) of His command to whom of His servants He wills (saying): 'Warn mankind that none has the right to be worshipped but I, so have Taqwa of Me'"* (16:2), and *"And truly, this is a revelation from the Lord of all that exists, which the trustworthy Ruh (Jibril) has brought down upon your heart that you may be one of the warners"* (26:192–194) — the trustworthy Rūḥ being Jibrīl. And the ayah says it comes **عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَاءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ**, "to any of His servants He wills": the choosing is His.

The entire purpose of that revelation is then given in one clause: **لِيُنذِرَ يَوْمَ التَّلَاقِ**, *"that he may warn of the Day of Mutual Meeting."* 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Day of Mutual Meeting is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection, of which Allah warns His servants." Ibn Kathir adds: that is the Day when everyone will find out about his deeds, good and bad.

## Ayah 16 — out in the open, and one question

*"The Day when they will come out, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"*

**بَارِزُونَ** (*bārizūn*) means coming out into plain view. Ibn Kathir: they will all appear in the open, with nothing to give them shelter or shade, or cover them. Maarif ul Quran fills in the scene — on the Day of Resurrection the land surface will be turned into a single level, without any mountains, caves, trees or buildings that could obstruct the view, so that everyone will be in an open expanse, open to view.

Then: *nothing of them will be hidden from Allah*, which Ibn Kathir explains as everything being equally known to Him. Read carefully, this is not saying that Allah's knowledge increases on that Day — everything is equally known to Him. What ends that Day is the *concealment*: the coverings people lived behind fall away, and they stand knowing that they are seen.

And into that exposure comes the question: **لِّمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ** — *"Whose is the kingdom this Day?"* Ibn Kathir recalls the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that Allah will roll up the heavens and the earth in His Hand and will say: *"I am the King, I am the Compeller, I am the Proud, where are the kings of the earth? Where are the tyrants? Where are the proud?"* — words we affirm as they came, without asking how and without explaining them away. And in the hadith about the Trumpet, it says that Allah will take the souls of all of His creatures, and there will be none left but Him Alone, with no partner or associate; then He will say, "Whose is the kingdom today?" three times, and He will answer Himself: *"It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"* Ibn Kathir glosses **الْقَهَّار** (*al-Qahhār*) as the Only One who has subjugated all things.

### When is the question asked?

Here the commentators genuinely differ, and Maarif ul Quran presents both positions:

- **After the second blowing of the Horn**, once everyone has been raised. This suits the flow of the passage: "the Day of Meeting" and "the Day they will come out in open view" both come after the second blast, with the level surface put in place, so the statement would come after everyone has been raised again. Al-Qurtubi has presented a hadith in support with reference to Nahhas, reported by Abu Wa'il from 'Abdullah Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): all human beings will be assembled together on a clear surface, a surface on which no sin would have been committed by anyone, and a herald will be commanded to proclaim *"To whom belongs the kingdom today?"* — and the entire creation, believer or disbeliever, will respond, *"To Allah alone, the One, the All-Dominant."* The believers will be more than pleased to say so, for it is already part of their belief; the disbelievers will confess to it sadly and helplessly.
- **After the first blowing**, when the entire creation lies annihilated — even Jibra'il, Mika'il, Israfil and the angel of death having met death — and none remains but Allah. Since there will be no one left to answer, He will Himself answer. Hasan al-Basri said that in this situation the One asking the question and the One responding to it is no other than Allah alone. Muhammad Ibn Ka'b al-Qurai also says this.

*Tafsir Ad-Durr-ul-Manthur*, after reporting narrations of both kinds, says it is possible that this statement is made twice — once at the annihilation of the existing universe after the first blowing, and once after the whole creation has been brought back to life at the second. Maulana Ashraf Thanavi said in *Bayan-ul-Qur'an* that the tafsir of the Qur'an does not hinge on declaring that it is made twice: it is also possible that the ayah is mentioning what comes to pass after the first blowing, referred to here among the events of the second as a reminder of what happened before. And Allah knows best.

## Ayah 17 — paid in full, wronged by no one

*"This Day shall every person be recompensed for what he earned. This Day no injustice. Truly, Allah is swift in reckoning."*

**بِمَا كَسَبَتْ** — *for what it earned.* The recompense is tied to a person's own earning, which is precisely why it can be perfectly fair.

Ibn Kathir explains this as Allah telling us of His justice when He judges between His creation: He does not do even a speck of dust's weight of injustice, whether it be for good or for evil. And then he shows what "no injustice" actually looks like — it is not cold symmetry. **For every good deed He gives a tenfold reward, and for every bad deed He gives the recompense of one bad deed.** The scales are honest, and they are tilted in your favour.

On **لَا ظُلْمَ الْيَوْمَ** ("This Day no injustice"), Ibn Kathir cites what was reported in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah said:

> "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself, and made it unlawful for you, so do not commit injustice to one another …" up to: "O My servants, these are your deeds, I record them for you then I will recompense you for them. Whoever finds something good, let him give praise to Allah, and whoever finds something other than that, let him blame no one but himself."

Two things sit in that hadith at once. Allah has forbidden injustice **for Himself** — the guarantee that the Day will be fair comes from Him, not from anything imposed on Him from outside. And the closing line seals off every excuse: on that Day, praise and self-blame are the only two responses left.

**إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الْحِسَابِ** — *"Truly, Allah is swift in reckoning."* Ibn Kathir: He will bring all His creation to account as if He is bringing just one person to account. This is like *"The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as a single person"* (31:28), and *"And Our commandment is but one as the twinkling of an eye"* (54:50). Do not picture a queue stretching over the horizon while you wait your turn; numbers are no burden on Him.

## Living it

Ayah 14 is the passage's one imperative, and everything around it exists to make that imperative reasonable. The signs and the rain in ayah 13 tell you who has been providing for you all along. The Throne and the revelation in ayah 15 tell you who has been guiding. The open plain of ayah 16 tells you that the audience you were performing for will not be there. And the reckoning in ayah 17 tells you that the only ledger to be read is one you wrote yourself.

So the practical shape of these ayat is small and daily: read the ordinary world as evidence rather than scenery, keep your worship undiluted in belief and in conduct alike, and let it stay undiluted even when the people around you dislike it. And take the practice Ibn Kathir records after the prayer — close your prayer by saying the words of ayah 14 back to Allah, so that the sincerity being asked of you is the last thing on your tongue before you stand up and re-enter the world.

passages.title: The Approaching Day, when no intercessor is obeyed
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single warning that the Prophet ﷺ is told to deliver: a Day is coming, it is close, and on it every escape route a person quietly relies on will be gone. What holds ayat 18–20 together is that they close those routes one by one — no rescue from another creature (ayah 18), no hiding anything from Allah (ayah 19), and no rival authority who could overturn His verdict (ayah 20). The passage moves from terror, to exposure, to judgement.

## "The approaching Day"

Allah does not name it here "the Day of Resurrection" or "the Hour." He calls it **يَوْمَ الْآزِفَةِ** — *yawm al-āzifah*, the approaching Day. Ibn Kathir explains that "the Day that is drawing near" is one of the names of the Day of Judgement, and that it is so called because it is close.

To show that this is the Qur'an's settled way of speaking about it, Ibn Kathir gathers a string of verses that say the same thing in different words:

- "The Day of Resurrection draws near. None besides Allah can avert it" (53:57–58)
- "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been cleft asunder" (54:1)
- "Draws near for mankind their reckoning" (21:1)
- "The Event (the Hour) ordained by Allah will come to pass, so seek not to hasten it" (16:1)

And to that list he adds the moment the distance finally closes: "But when they will see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieve will change and turn black with sadness and in grief" (67:27).

## Hearts at the throats

**إِذِ الْقُلُوبُ لَدَى الْحَنَاجِرِ كَاظِمِينَ** — "when the hearts will be at the throats, *kāẓimīn*."

The image is physical and precise. Qatadah said of it: "When the hearts reach the throats because of fear, and they will neither come out nor go back to their places." Ibn Kathir records that ʿIkrimah, as-Suddi and others held the same view. The heart is dislodged by terror and lodged in the throat — it cannot escape the body and be done with it, and it cannot settle back down. On Qatadah's description, the dread has no exit and no relief.

The word **كَاظِمِينَ** (*kāẓimīn*) is read in more than one way:

**Silent.** Ibn Kathir glosses *kāẓimīn* as meaning silent, "for no one will speak without His permission," and supports this with 78:38: "The Day that Ar-Rūḥ (Jibrīl) and the angels will stand forth in rows, they will not speak except him whom the Most Gracious allows, and he will speak what is right." On this reading it is not merely that no one dares to speak; no one *may* — speech itself waits on Allah's permission.

**Weeping.** Ibn Jurayj said *kāẓimīn* "means weeping." The two readings sit together well: grief with the sound pressed back down inside.

## No friend, no intercessor who is obeyed

**مَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ حَمِيمٍ وَلَا شَفِيعٍ يُطَاعُ** — "There will be no friend, nor an intercessor for the wrongdoers, who could be given heed to."

Ibn Kathir is careful about who is being described. "The wrongdoers" here, he says, are "those who wronged themselves by associating others in worship with Allah." Of them he says: they "will have no relative to help them and no intercessor who can plead on their behalf; all means of good will be cut off from them."

Two lifelines are named and both are cut — the relative who would help you because you are his, and the intercessor who would plead for you. Between them they cover the two ways human beings normally survive a court: someone who is on your side, and someone whose word carries weight.

Note also the exact wording: not merely "no intercessor," but no intercessor **يُطَاعُ** — "who could be given heed to," whose word would be acted upon. And this follows directly on *kāẓimīn* in the same ayah, which Ibn Kathir explained by the principle that no one will speak without Allah's permission.

## The eye that betrays

Then, in ayah 19, the passage turns from the scene of that Day to something happening right now, inside you: **يَعْلَمُ خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ** — "Allah knows the fraud of the eyes, and all that the breasts conceal."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders *khā'inat al-aʿyun* as "the treachery of the eyes — in other words, eyes that betray the trust." Sight, on that reading, is something entrusted, and the eye that misuses it is committing a small act of betrayal. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the phrase as the action of someone who secretly and surreptitiously casts a glance at something forbidden to him — for instance, a glance of sexual desire at a person he has no right to look at that way — and then takes the glance away if anyone is around, or aims it in a manner nobody notices. The whole skill of it is the concealment. And "all these things are open before Allah Taʿālā."

The early authorities open the phrase wider still:

- **Ad-Daḥḥāk**: it is "a wink, and a man saying that he has seen something when he has not seen it, or saying that he has not seen it when he did see it." So it is not only the lustful glance — it takes in the winks and small visual lies with which people deceive one another.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him): "Allah knows when the eye looks at something, whether it wants to commit an act of betrayal or not." Ibn Kathir notes Mujāhid and Qatādah held this too. That is a searching standard: Allah knows the intention behind the glance — the difference between a look that merely lands on something and a look that is reaching for it. As Ibn Kathir puts it, He knows the fraud of the eyes "even if the eyes look innocent."

And then the second half — **وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ**, "all that the breasts conceal" — goes past behaviour altogether into the sealed room of the self. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said of it: "He knows, if you were able to, whether you would commit *zinā* with a woman or not" — that is, He knows what you would do if only the opportunity were there. As-Suddi said it means "insinuating whispers," the private suggestions the chest keeps to itself.

**Why this is placed here.** Ibn Kathir gives the purpose plainly: Allah is telling us of "His complete knowledge which encompasses all things, great and small, major and minor," and He tells us this "so that people will take note that He knows about them and they will have the proper sense of shyness before Allah. They will pay attention to the fact that He can see them." That shyness before Allah is the intended fruit of the ayah.

This is the hinge of the whole passage. Ayah 18 says nobody will be able to speak for you. Ayah 19 says there is nothing to be spoken *about* that He does not already know. The two together dismantle the quiet assumption behind most private sin: that it went unrecorded, and that it can be smoothed over later by someone or something.

## Allah judges with truth — and nothing else judges at all

**وَاللَّهُ يَقْضِي بِالْحَقِّ** — "And Allah judges with truth." Ibn Kathir: it means "He judges with justice." A judge whose knowledge encompasses all things, great and small, is a judge who can weigh everything.

The counterpart follows immediately: **وَالَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ لَا يَقْضُونَ بِشَيْءٍ** — "while those to whom they invoke besides Him, cannot judge anything." Ibn Kathir identifies these as the idols and false gods, and reads *lā yaqḍūna bi-shay'* as: "they do not possess anything and they cannot judge anything." They own nothing and decide nothing. Set beside "Allah judges with truth," the contrast is total — one Judge with everything, and a crowd of invoked names with nothing, not even a share.

Notice how the argument has come full circle. Ayah 18 denied the wrongdoers an intercessor who would be obeyed; ayah 20 names who those hoped-for intercessors actually are, and why they were never going to help: something that cannot judge anything cannot secure anything for you.

## The All-Hearer, the All-Seer

The passage seals with **إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ** — "Certainly, Allah! He is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer." Allah closes by naming Himself with two of His own names.

Ibn Kathir notes that this is how Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) interpreted the closing, and he cites alongside it 53:31, "that He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done, and reward those who do good, with what is best." In the same vein, al-Aʿmash narrated from Saʿīd bin Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that "And Allah judges with truth" means: "He is able to reward those who do good with good and those who do evil with evil."

And Ibn Kathir explains the two names themselves: "He hears all that His creatures say and He knows all about them, so He guides whomsoever He wills and sends astray whomsoever He wills. And He judges with perfect justice in all of that." Everything the passage has raised — hidden looks, hidden whispers, invoked names — stands under that hearing and that seeing.

## Living it

**Guard the glance.** The passage's own worked example, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it, is the sideways look timed so that nobody notices — and it calls that a betrayal of a trust. The habit the ayah is building is not paranoia but the "proper sense of shyness before Allah" that Ibn Kathir names: he says the very reason Allah tells us about His encompassing knowledge is so that we would feel it.

**Take the inner life seriously.** Ibn ʿAbbās's reading — that Allah knows what you would do if you were able to — is sobering, but it sits inside Ibn Kathir's larger point: Allah's knowledge "encompasses all things, great and small, major and minor." The same knowledge that reaches the concealed sin reaches everything else that is concealed, including what a person quietly resists.

**Do not build on intercessors who cannot be obeyed.** Whatever a person invokes besides Allah — the idols and false gods Ibn Kathir names here — "cannot judge anything." The only sound reliance is on the One who both knows the case and passes the verdict.

**And treat the Day as near.** The name Allah chose for it in ayah 18 is itself the argument: the approaching Day. Ibn Kathir says it is called that for the simplest of reasons — because it is close.

passages.title: Past nations' ruin and Pharaoh's threat to Moses
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat put two witnesses on the stand against the Quraysh who were rejecting the Prophet ﷺ: the silent ruins of nations that were stronger than they were, and the living record of Pharaoh, who threatened the life of a messenger sent to him with clear proof. Ayat 21–22 point outward to the destroyed civilisations whose traces are scattered across the land; ayat 23–27 zoom in on one court in Egypt, where Pharaoh threatens to kill Moses and Moses answers not with a threat but with a prayer. What binds the two halves is a single claim: strength that stands against Allah's messengers is not strength at all.

## Ayat 21–22: an argument you can walk through

"Have they not traveled in the land and seen what was the end of those who were before them?" Ibn Kathir reads this as addressed directly to the deniers among the Quraysh — *these people who disbelieve in your Message, O Muhammad*. It is not an invitation to sightseeing but to inference. The Qur'an asks them to do two things in sequence: **travel** (*yasīrū*), then **look** (*fa-yanẓurū*) — and the looking is not with the eye alone, but at *ʿāqibah*, the **end** or outcome of a people. Anyone can see a ruin. The Qur'an asks them to see a verdict.

And what were those nations? Ibn Kathir explains: the nations of the past who disbelieved in their Prophets (peace be upon them), upon whom the punishment came **even though they were stronger than Quraysh**. The ayah names two measures of that superiority — strength, and *āthār fī al-arḍ*, "traces in the land." Ibn Kathir glosses the traces as "structures, buildings and dwellings which these people cannot match," and brings two other ayat as parallels: *"And indeed We had firmly established them with that wherewith We have not established you"* (46:26), and *"and they tilled the earth and populated it in greater numbers than these have done"* (30:9). This is a deliberately humbling comparison: the very people whose remains they pass were their superiors in every worldly index — "yet despite this great strength, Allah punished them for their sin, which was their disbelief in their Messengers."

**"And none had they to protect them from Allah."** The word is *wāq* — a shield, a guard. Ibn Kathir: "they had no one who could protect them or ward off the punishment from them." Note where the emptiness lies. It is not that they lacked armies or allies; they had more of both than Quraysh. It is that no created thing can stand between a person and Allah when Allah's decree comes.

## Why they were seized (ayah 22)

Ayah 21 states the sentence; ayah 22 opens the file and reads out the charge. Ibn Kathir marks the transition: "Then Allah mentions the reason why He punished them, and the sins which they committed." The charge is not that they were rich, or arrogant in the abstract. It is precisely this: **"there came to them their Messengers with clear evidences but they disbelieved."**

*Al-bayyināt* — Ibn Kathir renders it "clear proof and definitive evidence." The point of the word is that nothing was withheld from them. They were not condemned for failing to guess; they were condemned for refusing what had been made plain. "But they disbelieved" means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that "despite all these signs, they disbelieved and rejected the Message." *Fa-akhadhahumu Allāh* — "So Allah seized them" — he explains as "He destroyed them utterly, **and a similar fate awaits the disbelievers**." That last clause is the hinge of the whole passage: the ruins are not only history, they are a forecast.

**The ayah closes on Allah Himself.** He is *Qawiyy*, All-Strong — Ibn Kathir: "He is possessed of great strength and might." And He is *Shadīd al-ʿiqāb*, Severe in punishment — "His punishment is severe and agonising." Ibn Kathir does not pass over this coldly; he interrupts his own commentary to pray, "we seek refuge with Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, from that." We affirm these as Allah has described Himself, without likening His strength to the strength of creatures and without emptying the words of their meaning. And notice the placement: *Qawiyy* stands immediately after a survey of the strongest people who ever built anything. Their strength was real; His is of another order entirely.

## Ayat 23–27: why Moses appears here

Both commentaries agree on the purpose of the shift. Ibn Kathir: "Allah consoles His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for the disbelief of his people and gives him the glad tidings of good consequences and victory in this world and the Hereafter, as happened to Musa bin ʿImran, peace be upon him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same with the human texture filled in: the repeated warnings to the deniers of pure monotheism and prophethood "brought more opposition and hostility from disbelievers. Naturally, this situation made the Holy Prophet ﷺ sad. It was to comfort him that... mentioned there is the story of Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) and Pharaoh."

So this is not a change of subject. It is comfort delivered as history. *You are not the first, and the pattern does not end where they think it ends.*

**"And indeed We sent Musa with Our Ayat, and a manifest authority" (ayah 23).** On *sulṭān mubīn*, Ibn Kathir is brief and precise: "Authority means proof and evidence." That is worth pausing on. What Moses is armed with, in the Qur'an's own accounting, is *demonstrated truth* — and the Qur'an calls it *mubīn*, clear and self-evidencing. Two kinds of authority are about to collide in that court, and we have already been told which one the Qur'an dignifies with that word.

*(A note on the wider scene: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that these ayat open a longer passage containing "a lengthy dialogue between the Pharaoh, his people and a righteous elder who, despite being a scion of the House of the Pharaoh, had believed in the faith of Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) after having seen the miracles shown at his hands — but had kept his faith secret until that time." The early authorities Muqātil, Suddī and Ḥasan held that he was Pharaoh's cousin, and the same man who — when the court was discussing killing Moses in retaliation for the killing of the Copt — "had come running from the far side of the city" to warn him and advise him to leave Egypt: the incident of "And there came a man running, from the farthest part of the city" (28:20). On his name, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān corrects a common confusion: some sources call him Ḥabīb, but Ḥabīb is properly the man mentioned in Sūrah Yā Sīn (36:20). This man's name is given as **Shamʿān**, which Suhaylī considers most correct; others say **Hizqil**, which Thaʿlabī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him). And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays, on the authority of Qurṭubī, that the Prophet ﷺ named among the ṣiddīqīn — the truthful ones — Ḥabīb the carpenter whose incident appears in Sūrah Yā Sīn, the believer from the House of Pharaoh, and Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), "and he is the foremost among them.")*

## The three men (ayah 24)

Moses is sent "to Fir'awn, Hāmān and Qārūn." Ibn Kathir identifies each: **Fir'awn**, "the king of the Copts of Egypt"; **Hāmān**, "his adviser"; **Qārūn**, "the richest trader among the people of his time." Sovereign power, political counsel, and concentrated wealth — three pillars a worldly order rests on, all named in one breath and all on the same side.

Their answer is two words: *sāḥirun kadhdhāb*, "a sorcerer, a liar." Ibn Kathir explains that they "rejected him and thought he was a sorcerer, a madman and an illusionist who was telling lies about having been sent by Allah." Then he shows the Quraysh their own faces in it, quoting: *"Likewise, no Messenger came to those before them but they said: 'A sorcerer or a madman!' Have they transmitted this saying to these? Nay, they are themselves a people transgressing beyond bounds!"* (51:52–53). The slander is not even original. Every generation of rejecters reaches for the same two accusations — *he is doing tricks* and *he is making it up* — as though they had passed the script down to one another.

## Ayah 25: killing the sons, a second time

"Then, when he brought them the Truth from Us, they said: 'Kill with him the sons of those who believe and let their women live.'"

Ibn Kathir explains that **this was a second command** from Pharaoh to kill the males of the Children of Israel. "The first command had been as a precaution against the emergence of a man like Musa, or an act intended to humiliate this people or reduce their numbers or both. The second command was for the second reason, to humiliate the people so that they would regard Musa as a bad omen." That is a chillingly intelligent cruelty. Pharaoh cannot refute the signs, so he engineers suffering and lets the Israelites blame the messenger for it: *life was bearable until he came.*

And the Qur'an itself records that this is exactly what happened. Ibn Kathir cites the Children of Israel's complaint: *"We had suffered troubles before you came to us, and since you have come to us." He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors on the earth, so that He may see how you act?"* (7:129). Qatādah said this was "one command after another."

Then the divine verdict cuts across the scheme: **"but the plots of disbelievers are nothing but in vain."** *Kayd* is scheming — the clever, hidden move. Ibn Kathir: "their schemes and intentions — to reduce the numbers of the Children of Israel lest they prevail over them — were doomed to failure." Read from inside the story, Pharaoh's plan looks unstoppable. The ayah files it, while it is still in progress, under *ḍalāl*: lost, going nowhere.

## Ayah 26: the tyrant's performance

"Fir'awn said: 'Leave me to kill Musa, and let him call his Lord!'"

*Dharūnī* — "leave me alone, let me at him." Ibn Kathir: Pharaoh "resolved to kill Musa, peace be upon him, i.e., he said to his people, 'let me kill him for you.'" There is something strange in the king of Egypt asking his own people for room to act. It reads as performance — a display of restraint he is not actually exercising, so that the killing looks like a service rendered to them rather than the panic it is.

**"And let him call his Lord!"** Ibn Kathir gives the tone in four words: "I do not care." He calls this "the utmost in offensive stubbornness." Pharaoh is not weighing the claim and rejecting it; he is waving it away. That is the specific disease this passage is about — not ignorance, but defiance in the face of clear evidence.

**"I fear that he may change your religion, or that he may cause mischief to appear in the land!"** Ibn Kathir explains the stated fear — Pharaoh "was afraid that Musa would lead his people astray and change their ways and customs" — and then punctures it with unmistakable irony: "As if Fir'awn would be concerned about what Musa might do to his people!" The man who has just ordered the killing of the sons of those who believe now presents himself as the protector of religion and public order. Ibn Kathir notes a fine point of reading too: "the majority understood this as meaning, 'he will change your religion **and** cause mischief to appear in the land'" — that is, the *or* is not a genuine hesitation between two possibilities but a piling-up of charges.

Tyranny still speaks this dialect. The truth is never opposed as truth; it is opposed as a threat to stability, to tradition, to the nation's way of life.

## Ayah 27: the answer of a prophet

"Musa said: 'Verily, I seek refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant who believes not in the Day of Reckoning!'"

A death threat has just been announced in open court, and Moses does not raise an army, negotiate, or answer the insult. Ibn Kathir: when he heard "Leave me to kill Musa," Moses "said, 'I seek refuge and protection with Allah from his evil and the evil of those like him.'" The whole of his reply is a turning toward Allah.

Three things in his words repay attention:

**"My Lord and your Lord."** Ibn Kathir notes that this is addressed to "those who were being addressed here" — the court itself. Standing in front of the men who have just discussed killing him, Moses is still calling them. He will not concede that Pharaoh owns them. The Lord he takes shelter with is *their* Lord too, whether they acknowledge it or not.

**"Every arrogant one" (*mutakabbir*).** He does not say "from Pharaoh." Ibn Kathir glosses the word as "every evildoer," and the generality is the point: the refuge is sought from a type, not a name. Pharaoh is one instance of something that keeps recurring — which is exactly why this story is being told to console the Prophet ﷺ while his own people rejected him, and why it still reads as current.
