**"Who believes not in the Day of Reckoning."** This is the diagnosis underneath the arrogance. A man who genuinely expects a day of accounting cannot make himself the final authority. Denying *yawm al-ḥisāb* is what licenses everything Pharaoh has just said.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a report narrated from Abu Musa (may Allah be pleased with him) that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was afraid of some people, he would say: *"O Allah, we seek refuge in You from their evil and we seek Your help in repulsing them."* The Prophet ﷺ met threat the way Moses met it — by taking shelter in Allah — which is itself part of the consolation these ayat were sent to give him. The passage that began with ruined nations who had no protector ends with a prophet, under a death sentence, holding fast to the only protection there is.

## Living it

**Read ruins as arguments.** Ayah 21 makes travel a form of reflection. Every fallen power whose remains we photograph was, in its day, more established than we are. The question the Qur'an trains us to ask of any impressive power is not "how did they build this?" but "how did they end?"

**Take the charge in ayah 22 personally.** The sin that destroyed them was clear evidence, met with refusal. Whoever has the Qur'an in front of him has *bayyināt*. The danger is never being under-informed; it is knowing and turning away.

**Answer intimidation with refuge, not with matching force.** Moses' response in ayah 27 is the model, and the Prophet's ﷺ practice was the same. Seeking refuge is not passivity — it is relocating your protection from what cannot protect (ayah 21: they had no *wāq*) to the One who can.

**Watch for the *mutakabbir* in yourself.** Moses sought refuge from a type, and the root of the type is named for us: not believing in the Day of Reckoning. To the degree the reckoning is real to a person, arrogance has nowhere left to stand.

passages.title: The hidden believer confronts Pharaoh's court
passages.tafsir:
Pharaoh has just said, "Leave me to kill Musa, peace be upon him." Into that moment a man stands up — a man of Pharaoh's own household who had kept his faith hidden from his people until this day. These eight ayat carry his speech: one sustained argument, interrupted once by Pharaoh, that begins as a plea to spare a man's life and ends with sealed hearts and the Day of Judgment. What holds the passage together is a single voice — the lone believer in a hostile court — moving from reason, to history, to the Hereafter, while the tyrant answers him with one sentence of pure self-assurance.

## The man who had been hiding

Ibn Kathir reports that the well-known view is that this believer was a Copt, an Egyptian of Pharaoh's own family. As-Suddi said he was Pharaoh's cousin — the son of his paternal uncle. It was also said that he was the one later saved along with Musa, peace be upon him.

Ibn Jurayj reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that no one from the family of Pharaoh believed except three: this man, Pharaoh's wife, and the man who said, "O Musa! Verily, the chiefs are taking counsel together about you, to kill you" (28:20). That report was narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Kathir notes that he concealed his faith from his people, the Egyptians, and did not reveal it until this day — the day Pharaoh announced his intention to kill Musa, peace be upon him. Ibn Kathir says the man "was seized with anger for the sake of Allah," and adds that the best of jihad is to speak a just word before an unjust ruler, as is stated in the Hadith; there is no greater example of it than what this man said to Pharaoh.

**A note on concealing faith.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a point of law from *yaktumu īmānahu* ("who was hiding his faith") in ayah 28: a person who does not announce his faith to people, yet is firm in it in his heart, is a believer. But it is established from clear textual authority of the Qur'an and Hadith that certitude of the heart alone is not enough for faith to be accepted — a verbal confession and declaration is a condition, and without it a person is not regarded as a believer. What is *not* required is making that declaration publicly. The only reason public knowledge matters is that until people know a person is Muslim, they cannot deal with him as they deal with Muslims (attributed to Qurtubi).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes what the phrase "a believing man from the House of Pharaoh" quietly demonstrates: in the dialogue that follows, this believer both invited Pharaoh and his people toward truth and faith, and restrained them from killing Sayyidnā Musa, peace be upon him.

## The shape of his argument (ayah 28)

He does not begin with "I believe." He begins with a question aimed at the conscience of the room: *a-taqtulūna rajulan an yaqūla rabbiya Allāh* — "Would you kill a man because he says: 'My Lord is Allah,' and he has come to you with clear signs from your Lord?" Ibn Kathir unpacks it as: how can you kill a man merely for saying "My Lord is Allah," when he has brought proof that what he says is true?

Then — the striking move — he steps out of his own conviction and argues on their terms. Ibn Kathir says he "went along with them for the sake of argument": *if he is a liar, the sin of his lie falls on him; and if he is truthful, some of what he threatens you with will strike you.* The logic leaves no exit. If Musa, peace be upon him, is lying, Allah will punish him for it in this world and the next — so you lose nothing by leaving him alone. If he is truthful and you harm him, some of the punishment he warns of will land on you. Either way, on Ibn Kathir's reading, plain common sense says: leave him and his people alone and do not harm them.

That request — *just leave us alone* — is exactly what Musa, peace be upon him, asked for: "Deliver to me the servants of Allah… But if you believe me not, then keep away from me and leave me alone" (44:17–21). Ibn Kathir draws the line forward: in the same way the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked the Quraysh to leave him alone and let him call the servants of Allah, appealing to the kinship between them — "Say: 'No reward do I ask of you for this except to be kind to me for my kinship with you'" (42:23), meaning, do not harm me because of the ties between us; let me address my call to the people. Ibn Kathir adds that this was the basis of the truce agreed at al-Hudaybiyah, which was a manifest victory.

**The closing clause of ayah 28** is easy to read past: "Verily, Allah guides not one who is a transgressor, a liar." Ibn Kathir reads it as the believer's final evidential point: if a man claiming to be sent by Allah were the liar you say he is, it would show — his words and deeds would be inconsistent and self-contradictory. But look at him: he is upright and what he says holds together. Had he been a sinner and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to speech and conduct as coherent as what you can see with your own eyes.

## Abu Bakr says the same sentence

Ibn Kathir sets a similar story beside this one. Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from 'Urwah bin az-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said to 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Tell me, what was the worst thing the idolators did to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?' He said, 'While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, 'Uqbah bin Abi Mu'it came and grabbed the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and started twisting his garment so that it strangled him. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, came and grabbed ['Uqbah's] shoulder and pushed him away from the Prophet ﷺ, then he said: *Would you kill a man because he says: "My Lord is Allah," and he has come to you with clear signs from your Lord?*'" This was recorded by Al-Bukhari.

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, standing between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the hands of an idolater, speaks the very words the believer of Pharaoh's house had spoken in Pharaoh's court.

## "Who will save us?" (ayah 29)

Having pleaded for Musa, peace be upon him, he now turns to his people's own interests. "O my people! Yours is the kingdom today, you being dominant in the land." Ibn Kathir reads this as a reminder of blessing: Allah has given you this kingdom, this dominance, this power and authority — so guard the blessing by thanking Allah and believing in His Messenger, and beware of Allah's punishment if you reject him.

Then notice the pronoun turn. He says "yours is the kingdom," but "who will save *us*?" He does not stand outside them as an accuser; he places himself under the same sky. Ibn Kathir's meaning: these soldiers and troops will avail you nothing and will not ward off Allah's punishment if He decides to punish.

**Pharaoh's answer** is the whole psychology of tyranny in one line: "I show you only that which I see, and I guide you only to the path of right policy." Ibn Kathir remarks, pointedly, that this was Pharaoh's reply "to the advice of this righteous man who was more deserving of kingship than Pharaoh." The first half means: I only tell you and advise you what I myself think is good. But Pharaoh lied — he knew Musa, peace be upon him, was truthful about the Message he brought. Musa, peace be upon him, had told him: "Verily, you know that these signs have been sent down by none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth" (17:102); and of such people Allah says, "And they belied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though they were themselves convinced thereof" (27:14). Ibn Kathir's verdict: Pharaoh uttered a lie and a fabrication, betrayed Allah and His Messenger, and cheated his people by not advising them sincerely. His claim to be guiding them to *sabīl ar-rashād*, the path of right guidance, was equally a lie — yet his people obeyed him and followed him: "they followed the command of Fir'awn, and the command of Fir'awn was no right guide" (11:97); "And Fir'awn led his people astray, and he did not guide them" (20:79).

Ibn Kathir closes this with a hadith, without naming its collection: that no leader dies having cheated his people except that he will never smell the fragrance of Paradise — and its fragrance is detected from a distance of a five-hundred-year journey.

## The warning from history (ayat 30–31)

Now the believer changes register. "I fear for you a day like the day of the *aḥzāb*" — the confederated groups, the coalitions of the past. Ayah 31 names them: the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, and those who came after them. Ibn Kathir explains: those earlier nations who rejected the Messengers of Allah, and how Allah's punishment came upon them with no one to protect them or ward it off.

Then the safeguard against a wrong conclusion: "And Allah wills no injustice for His servants." Ibn Kathir: Allah destroyed them for their sins and for their disbelief in and rejection of His Messengers — this was His command and decree concerning them, fulfilled.

## The Day of Calling (ayat 32–33)

Having warned of punishment in this world, he moves to the next: "I fear for you *yawm at-tanād*." Ibn Kathir: this is the Day of Resurrection.

**The word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *tanād*, with a kasrah on the *dāl*, is a shortened form of *tanādī*, which means *calling one another*. The Day of Judgment is named "the Day of Mutual Calling" because that terrible day will reverberate with countless calls and cries.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration of Sayyidnā 'Abdullah Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: when the Day of Qiyamah comes, an announcer from Allah will proclaim, "Let the adversaries of Allah stand" — meaning those who rejected *taqdīr*, divine predestination. Then the people of Jannah will call out to the people of Jahannam, and the people of Jahannam to the people of Jannah, and the people of al-A'rāf (the Heights) to both, each saying things about themselves. And names will be announced — of the fortunate and the unfortunate, along with their parentage, like an announcement of results declaring that so-and-so is successful and any misfortune for him is ruled out, and so-and-so unfortunate and any good fortune ruled out. (Reported by Ibn Abi Haim in As-Sunnah — Mazhari.)

Beside it stands a small, devastating scene: Sayyidnā Abu Hazim al-A'raj (may Allah be pleased with him) used to address his own self — "O A'raj, when the call comes on the Day of Qiyamah, 'Let those who committed such-and-such sins stand,' you will be standing with them; and at the next call, with them too…" — reckoning that at every sin announced he would have to stand, because he had all sorts of sins in store. (Reported by Abu Nu'aym — Mazhari.)

**"A Day when you will turn your backs and flee."** Ibn Kathir: running away — and then, "having no protector from Allah," meaning no one to shield you from His punishment. He sets beside it: "No! There is no refuge! Unto your Lord will be the place of rest that Day" (75:11–12).

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine difference among the commentators about *when* this fleeing happens:

- With reference to Imam al-Baghawi (via Bayān ul-Qur'an of Maulana Ashraf Thanavi), this describes the moment the guilty are taken away from the place of reckoning out towards Jahannam — that is, after all the calls and announcements of *yawm at-tanād* have been made, they are turned from the reckoning towards their final destination.
- Other commentators hold it describes the state of the world at the first blowing of the Horn: the earth cracks open, people start running in every direction, but there are angels at every outlet and no way out. On this view *yawm at-tanād* itself is the first blowing, since cries come from all corners then too. This reading is supported by another *qirāʾah* (recitation) reported from Sayyidnā Ibn 'Abbas and Dahhak, who read *yawm at-tanādd* with a doubled *dāl*, from *nadd*, meaning to run away — so "the Day of Fleeing," with ayah 33 as its explanation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a lengthy hadith found in Tafsir Mazhari, reported from Sayyidnā Abu Hurairah with reference to Ibn Jarir, Musnad Abu Ya'la, al-Baihaqi, Musnad 'Abd Ibn Humaid and others, mentioning three soundings of the Horn: the first causing consternation, the second unconsciousness, the third resurrection — and that at the blast of consternation people will be running about in panic, which is what Allah calls *yawm at-tanād*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends the discussion where an honest commentator should: "And Allah is Pure and High who knows best."

Ayah 33 closes with a line that reframes everything: "And whomsoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide." Ibn Kathir: whoever Allah sends astray has no guide other than Him.

## Yusuf, and the excuse of "no more messengers" (ayah 34)

The believer now reaches for something no one in that court could deny — their own national memory. Ibn Kathir explains that "Yusuf came to you, in times gone by, with clear signs" refers to the people of Egypt: Allah had sent them a Messenger before the time of Musa, peace be upon him, and it was Yusuf, peace be upon him, who attained a high position in their government. He called them to Allah with justice — but they obeyed him only in worldly matters connected to his office, and not in the worship of Allah.

Then: "you ceased not to doubt what he brought you, until when he died you said, 'No Messenger will Allah send after him.'" Ibn Kathir reads this as despair speaking, and wishful thinking — and traces it to their disbelief and their rejection of the Messengers. First doubt while the Messenger was among them; then, once he was gone, a comfortable doctrine that no one else would ever come — which is precisely the excuse they were now using against Musa, peace be upon him.

"Thus Allah leaves astray him who is a transgressor and a skeptic" — *musrif murtāb*. Ibn Kathir: this is the state of the one Allah sends astray because of his sinful actions and the doubts in his heart.

## Disputing without proof, and the sealed heart (ayah 35)

Ayah 35 describes them exactly: "Those who dispute about the Ayat of Allah without any authority that has come to them." Ibn Kathir: they attempt to refute truth with falsehood and argue against clear proof without any evidence or proof from Allah — and Allah hates them with the utmost loathing. The word *maqt* is strong: "it is greatly hateful and disgusting to Allah and to those who believe." Ibn Kathir notes both halves — the believers too come to despise such a person.

And the consequence: "Thus does Allah seal up the heart of every arrogant tyrant." Ibn Kathir: Allah puts a seal on such a heart so that after that it no longer acknowledges anything good or denounces anything evil — it cannot follow the truth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection to the scene itself: just as the hearts of Pharaoh and Haman remained unaffected by the good counsel of Sayyidnā Musa (peace be upon him) and of the believer from Pharaoh's house, so Allah seals the heart of every person who is arrogant and tyrannical — proud and oppressive. The effect is that the light of faith does not enter that heart, and the person becomes unable to distinguish good from bad. It also notes that in one *qirāʾah* the words for "arrogant" and "tyrant" are read as attributes of *the heart* itself, because the heart is the reservoir of all morals and deeds — every deed, good or bad, is born there. Hence the teaching, cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Qurtubi without naming a collection, that there is a piece of flesh in the body which, when it works right, makes the whole body work right, and when it goes bad, makes the whole body go bad.

## Living it

**Speak, even alone.** One man, inside Pharaoh's own household, who had kept his faith hidden until the day the killing was announced. He was, in Ibn Kathir's phrase, seized with anger for the sake of Allah — and Ibn Kathir places what he did in the highest rank: a just word before an unjust ruler.

**Argue like him.** He did not shout; he reasoned. He asked a question that made them hear their own intention. He granted his opponents their premise and showed that even on it, killing was indefensible. He appealed to their self-interest, to history, and only then to the Hereafter. And he never separated himself from them: "who will save *us*."

**Guard against the seal.** The diagnosis runs in a straight line through these ayat: doubt (34), then disputing without proof (35), then arrogance and tyranny — then the seal. The remedy is at the other end: submit to clear evidence when it reaches you, and keep the heart free of the pride that makes a man argue for a position rather than for the truth.

**Turn the ayat inward.** Abu Hazim al-A'raj addressed his own self about the calls of that Day, reckoning that at every sin announced he would have to stand. That instinct — hearing a warning as addressed to me — is the difference between reading this passage and being changed by it.

passages.title: Pharaoh's tower answered by the believer's call
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat set two voices side by side. Pharaoh answers Musa's message by ordering a tower into the sky, and the believing man from Pharaoh's own household answers Pharaoh by calling his people to the only road that actually leads somewhere. One man builds upward and gets nowhere; the other speaks plainly and points to the abode that lasts.

What holds the passage together is that both men claim to be showing the people the truth — and the Qur'an lets you watch which claim survives.

## The order for the tower (ayah 36)

Pharaoh calls to his minister: *ya Haman ibni li sarhan* — "O Haman, build me a tower." Ma'arif ul Qur'an explains that **sarh** means a structure that rises high. Ibn Kathir describes it as a tall, high, strong fortress, and notes that it was built of bricks made from baked clay — because elsewhere the Qur'an records Pharaoh's fuller instruction: "So kindle for me (a fire), O Haman, to bake (bricks out of) clay, and set up for me a lofty tower" (28:38).

Notice what that detail does. This is not a poetic gesture. It is a works order: fire the kilns, bake the clay, raise the levels. Pharaoh is putting the machinery of a state behind a claim about the unseen.

## "That I may arrive at the ways" (ayah 37)

His stated purpose is *la'alli ablughu al-asbab — asbaba as-samawat*, "that I may arrive at the ways — the ways of the heavens." Ibn Kathir reports from **Sa'id bin Jubayr** and **Abu Salih** that these are "the gates of the heavens"; it is also said, the ways or routes of the heavens. Either way the picture is of some access point to the sky that a high enough building might reach.

Then comes the real intent: *fa-attali'a ila ilahi Musa* — "and I may look upon the deity of Musa" — followed at once by *wa inni la-azunnuhu kadhiban*, "but verily, I think him to be a liar." Ibn Kathir's comment is exact: because of his disbelief and defiance, he did not believe that Allah had sent Musa to him. The verdict came first; the tower was only theatre arranged around a conclusion already reached.

**Was Pharaoh serious?** Ma'arif ul Qur'an weighs this honestly. Read plainly, the words suggest Pharaoh ordered a structure rising high enough into the sky for him to climb up, peek in, and have a glimpse of Allah. If a thought that wild — one not imaginable even in a man of very ordinary commonsense — really came from the sole master of the kingdom of Egypt, that is evidence of his unbelievable folly; and if his minister carried the order out, then as the king, so the courtier. Because nobody expects a head of state to go that far in his imagination, some commentators have said that Pharaoh knew perfectly well that no structure, however high, would let him reach the skies by that mode of ascent. He did it only to impress or confuse his people.

Ibn Kathir reads it the same way when he explains *wa kadhalika zuyyina li-Fir'awna su'u 'amalihi wa sudda 'ani as-sabil* — "Thus it was made fair seeming, in Fir'awn's eyes, the evil of his deeds, and he was hindered from the path." That refers, he says, to this very act of building the tower, by which Pharaoh wanted to deceive his people and make them think he could prove that Musa was lying.

So the tower is a piece of political stagecraft. Nobody was going to reach the gates of heaven with baked bricks. But the crowd watching the scaffolding go up is meant to feel that the question of Allah is being *handled* — that the state has the matter in hand and Musa's claim is under investigation. It is disbelief dressed up as due diligence.

**"And the plot of Fir'awn led to nothing but loss and destruction."** *Wa ma kaydu Fir'awna illa fi tabab.* Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid glossed *tabab* as "nothing but ruin." The phrase closes the file on the whole project: all that scheming did not fail partway, it was never anywhere except in ruin.

## Was the tower ever actually built?

Ma'arif ul Qur'an is careful here, and its care is worth imitating: **we have no sound and strong report proving whether or not such a palatial high structure was ever raised.** However, al-Qurtubi reports that the building was constructed, but that once it reached its higher levels it collapsed.

Then comes a striking observation. The author of Ma'arif ul Qur'an relates it from his own father, Maulana Muhammad Yasin — a dear disciple of Maulana Muhammad Ya'qub, the first principal of the famous Darul-'Uloom of Deoband in India — who reported his teacher saying: for that lofty palace to collapse, it is not necessary that it was struck by some divine punishment. The height of any building depends on the capacity of its foundation to bear weight. However deep a foundation is laid, it cannot go deeper than a certain limit. So as level after level was added, it was inevitable that once the load exceeded what the foundation could carry, the structure had to come down. That, he concludes, is a further proof of the folly of Pharaoh and Haman — and Allah knows best.

Two things are beautiful about this. First, the restraint: a scholar declines to reach for a miracle when ordinary physics explains the event, and still ends with *Allah knows best*. Second, the image it leaves you with — a foundation that can only go so deep, holding up an ambition that keeps going higher. That is Pharaoh's whole life in one sentence.

## The believer speaks (ayah 38)

Against all that noise, a man speaks. Ibn Kathir titles this section "More of what the Believer from Fir'awn's Family said," and describes his audience precisely: **his people, who persisted in their rebellion and transgression, and preferred the life of this world.**

*Ya qawmi ittabi'uni ahdikum sabila ar-rashad* — "O my people! Follow me, I will guide you to the way of right conduct."

Ibn Kathir points out the sharp edge here: this stands **in contrast to the false claim of Fir'awn**, who had said *wa ma ahdikum illa sabila ar-rashad* — "and I guide you only to the path of right policy." Look at the Arabic and you can see it: *sabil ar-rashad*, the identical phrase, in both mouths. Pharaoh had already occupied the language of guidance. The believer does not invent a new vocabulary; he takes the same words back and puts truth inside them.

That is worth sitting with. Falsehood rarely announces itself as falsehood. It calls itself the sensible path, the right policy, the responsible course. The believer's answer is not a slogan war but a change of destination — and he tells you immediately what that destination is.

## Why the world had them (ayah 39)

Ibn Kathir says the believer then sought to make them shun this world, which they had preferred to the Hereafter, and which had prevented them from believing in the Messenger of Allah, Musa, peace be upon him.

*Ya qawmi innama hadhihi al-hayatu ad-dunya mata'* — "O my people! Truly, this life of the world is nothing but an enjoyment." Ibn Kathir's gloss on **mata'**: it is insignificant and fleeting, and soon it will diminish and pass away. Hear how the sentence is built — *nothing but* an enjoyment. It is not that the world has no pleasure in it; it is that pleasure is all it has, and that pleasure is on its way out.

*Wa inna al-akhirata hiya daru al-qarar* — "and verily, the Hereafter, that is the home that will remain forever." Ibn Kathir defines it as the abode which will never end and from which there will be no departure — then adds the sentence that removes any comfort from vagueness: **which will be either Paradise or Hell.**

So the believer is not merely saying the world is small; he is diagnosing why these people cannot hear Musa. Their unbelief is not really an intellectual problem. It is an attachment. They preferred the passing thing, and preference decides what a person is willing to believe. Pharaoh's tower belongs to the same disease: an enormous outlay of clay and labour, spent inside a world that is *mata'*, in order to avoid a message about the world that stays.

## The scale that never cheats (ayah 40)

Having named the two abodes, the believer names the rule by which people arrive at them.

*Man 'amila sayyi'atan fa-la yujza illa mithlaha* — "Whoever does an evil deed will not be requited except the like thereof." Ibn Kathir: **one like it.** Not more. Nobody is punished beyond what they earned; there is no inflation on the side of punishment.

*Wa man 'amila salihan min dhakarin aw untha wa huwa mu'minun fa-ula'ika yadkhuluna al-jannata yurzaquna fiha bi-ghayri hisab* — "and whosoever does a righteous deed, whether male or female, and is a true believer, such will enter Paradise, where they will be provided therein without limit." Ibn Kathir explains *bi-ghayri hisab*: **the reward cannot be enumerated; Allah will give an immense reward without end.**

Feel the deliberate imbalance. Evil is capped at its own size. Good is uncapped. Justice is measured out to the last grain, and then generosity is let loose with no measure at all. That is not a tension in the ayah; it is the point of the ayah.

Two conditions frame the promise, and both matter. **"Whether male or female"** — the door is stated as open to both by name, not left to inference. And **"and is a true believer"** — the deed is carried by faith. Righteous action and faith travel together here; the ayah joins them rather than offering either on its own.

Ibn Kathir closes this section with a line worth keeping: **And Allah is the Guide to the straight path.** After a man has just said "follow me, I will guide you," the commentary quietly returns guidance to its Owner. The believer can call; only Allah guides.

## Living it

**Watch what you are building.** Pharaoh's project was not evil because it was tall. It was evil because it was a way of not answering. When we throw activity, expense, and cleverness at a question we already know the answer to, we are laying bricks on Haman's foundation.

**Check who has borrowed your vocabulary.** Pharaoh said "the path of right conduct" first. Names are cheap; destinations are not. Ask of any path offered to you where it ends, not what it is called.

**Ask which world your choices assume.** The people around the believer were not stupid. They preferred — and preference closed their ears. Every decision quietly declares whether you take this life to be *mata'*, a fleeting enjoyment, or the home that will remain forever.

**Take courage from the scale.** Nothing you did wrong will be exaggerated against you; anything you did rightly, with faith, is repaid on a scale that cannot be counted. And remember who said all of this out loud, alone, inside Pharaoh's own court, with the scaffolding of that tower going up behind him. Allah knows best.

passages.title: The believer's last appeal and Pharaoh's doom
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close the speech of the believing man from Pharaoh's own household and then show us how the argument ended — not in the court of Egypt, but in the sight of Allah. Ayat 41–44 are his last words to his people; ayat 45–46 are Allah's verdict on the two sides: one man rescued, a whole ruling house encircled by punishment that has not finished to this day.

What holds the passage together is a single contrast, drawn first by the man himself and then confirmed by Allah: two invitations, two destinations. He calls them to salvation; they call him to the Fire. He entrusts his affair to Allah; they lay plots. The last two ayat simply reveal which side was telling the truth.

## Two callers, two calls (ayat 41–42)

In ayah 41 the man puts his bewilderment as a question: *how is it* that he invites them to salvation while they invite him to the Fire? Ibn Kathir spells out what "salvation" (*najāh*) meant on his lips: "the worship of Allah alone with no partner or associate, and belief in His Messenger, whom He has sent." That is the whole of it. He is not offering a philosophy or a political programme; he is offering the one thing that saves.

Ayah 42 unpacks each side of the contrast. Their invitation is that he "disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him what I have no knowledge of." Ibn Kathir explains the phrase "of which I have no knowledge" as meaning that their creed rests "on the basis of ignorance, with no proof or evidence." Note how devastating that is as an argument: the man does not say their gods are inferior to Allah, he says there is nothing behind them — no proof, no evidence, nothing anyone can point to.

Against that he sets his own invitation: "and I invite you to **al-ʿAzīz al-Ghaffār** — the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving." The pairing of the two names is the heart of the ayah, and Ibn Kathir catches it exactly: "with all His might and pride, He still forgives the sin of the one who repents to Him." Among people, might and mercy usually pull apart — the strong are rarely forgiving, and the forgiving are often forgiving because they are weak. In Allah they are one. His forgiveness costs Him nothing of His power, and His power is never a reason to despair of His pardon. And notice who is being offered this: the very people he has just described as calling him to the Fire. The door named *al-Ghaffār* is being held open for them.

## "Lā jarama" — no doubt about it (ayah 43)

Ayah 43 opens with the arresting phrase **lā jarama**. The early authorities Ibn Kathir gathers read it in slightly different ways, all pointing the same direction:

- As-Suddi and Ibn Jarir: it means **"Truly."**
- Ad-Dahhak: it means **"No lie."**
- ʿAli bin Abi Talhah and Ibn ʿAbbas: "Indeed, the one that you call me to, of idols and false gods, has no claim in this world or in the Hereafter."

So the man moves from a question (ayah 41) to a flat certainty. Whatever residual doubt his listeners might have expected of him, he shuts the door: *no doubt at all* about what these objects of worship are.

And what are they? The ayah says they have no *daʿwah* — no claim, no call that answers — "in this world or in the Hereafter." The early commentators fill this in from different angles:

- **Mujahid:** "The idols that do not have anything."
- **Qatadah:** "Idols possess no power either to benefit or to harm."
- **As-Suddi:** "They do not respond to those who call upon them, either in this world or in the Hereafter."

Ibn Kathir then reads the point against two other passages of the Qur'an. First, "And who is more astray than one who calls on besides Allah such as will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their calls to them? And when the people are gathered, they will become their enemies and deny their worship" (46:5–6). Second, "If you invoke them, they hear not your call; and if they were to hear, they could not grant it to you" (35:14). Put together, the picture is complete: in this life the false god cannot hear; if it could hear it could not help; and in the next life it turns on its own worshipper.

The second half of ayah 43 states the alternative in one line: "our return will be to Allah." Ibn Kathir: this is "in the Hereafter, where He will reward or punish each person according to his deeds." And then the closing clause — "and the *musrifūn*, the transgressors, they shall be the dwellers of the Fire." Ibn Kathir notes they will "dwell therein forever, because of their great sin, which is associating others in worship with Allah." The believer is not calling names; he is naming a category and letting his listeners see whether they belong to it.

## "I entrust my affair to Allah" (ayah 44)

Ayah 44 is the hinge of the whole passage, and it has two halves that every believer under pressure should learn.

**"You will remember what I am telling you."** Ibn Kathir: 'you will come to know the truth of what I enjoined upon you and forbade you, the advice I gave you and what I explained to you. You will come to know, and you will feel regret at the time when regret will be of no avail.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same and fixes the timing: if they will not listen now, a time will come when the punishment seizes them and they *will* remember what he told them — and remembering then will be useless to them. This is one of the most sobering things a caller to truth can say. He does not claim he will win the argument. He says the argument is already decided, and they will find that out at the wrong moment.

**"And I entrust my affair to Allah."** The verb here — *ufawwiḍu amrī* — is the language of handing a case over completely. Ibn Kathir glosses it in two movements: 'I put my trust in Allah and seek His help, **and I renounce you utterly**.' Both are there: attachment to Allah and detachment from them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human situation that produced the sentence: after this lengthy dialogue, advice and invitation, his faith now stood disclosed before these people, and he realised they might bring some harm to him — so he left his case to rest with Allah, who is the guardian and protector of His servants. This is not a serene phrase spoken from safety. It is what a man says when he has just made himself a target and has nowhere else to go.

The ayah ends with a name: **"Indeed, Allah is All-Seeing (Baṣīr) of His servants."** Ibn Kathir draws out what it means for the man's situation: "He knows all about them, may He be exalted and sanctified, and He guides those who deserve to be guided and sends astray those who deserve to be sent astray; His is the perfect proof, utmost wisdom and mighty power." A man surrounded by enemies who cannot be reasoned with is telling himself: the One who sees is enough.

## Allah's verdict (ayah 45)

Ayah 45 answers ayah 44 almost word for word. He entrusted his affair — "So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted." Ibn Kathir says this protection covered "this world and the Hereafter": in this world Allah saved him along with Musa, peace be upon him, and in the Hereafter He will admit him to Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful about the details: the Qur'an does not mention exactly what the plots were, only that the people of Pharaoh had made many plans to hurt and kill him, and that when Pharaoh's people were drowned, Allah saved this believing servant along with Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him). As for his salvation in the Hereafter, it says, that is fairly obvious. It also records from the early tafsir authority **Muqatil** that when Pharaoh's people came after him, as he had feared, he escaped towards the mountains and they could not catch him.

Then the other half of the ledger: "and the House of Pharaoh was encircled by an evil punishment." Ibn Kathir explains the sequence — this "refers to drowning in the sea, then being transferred from there to Hell." Those who had planned to seize one man were themselves seized.

## The Fire, morning and evening (ayah 46)

Ayah 46 is one of the most weighty verses in the Qur'an on what happens between death and the Resurrection. Two stages are named.

**Now:** "The Fire, they are exposed to it, morning and evening." Ibn Kathir: their souls are exposed to the Fire morning and evening until the Hour begins. **Qatadah** said of "morning and evening": "every morning and every evening, for as long as this world remains, it will be said to them by way of rebuke and humiliation: O people of Fir'awn, this is your position." **Ibn Zayd** said, "They are there today, being exposed to it morning and evening, until the Hour begins" — and in the same passage he says the people of Fir'awn are "like foolish camels, stumbling into rocks and trees without thinking." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an explanation of the ayah from **Sayyidna ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿūd**: the spirits of people from the House of Pharaoh are presented before Jahannam in the form of black birds, twice every day, morning and evening, and Jahannam is pointed out to them with the words: this is your abode (reported by Abd-ur-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Haim — Mazhari).

**Then:** "And on the Day when the Hour is established: Admit the people of Fir'awn into the severest torment." Ibn Kathir: on that Day "their souls and bodies will be reunited in Hell," and "the severest torment" means "more intense pain and greater agony." What they are shown daily now is not yet the thing itself; it is the doorway.

### The scholars' discussion: punishment in the grave

Ibn Kathir says this ayah "contains one of the major proofs used by the Ahlus-Sunnah to prove that there will be torment in the grave during the period of Al-Barzakh" — the interval between a person's death and the Resurrection. He then raises the objection honestly rather than sweeping it aside: this ayah was undoubtedly revealed in Makkah, yet a well-known narration suggests the Prophet ﷺ came to speak of the punishment of the grave only later.

That narration is recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from **ʿA'ishah**, may Allah be pleased with her. A Jewish woman used to serve her and would say, whenever ʿA'ishah did her a favour, "May Allah save you from the torment of the grave." ʿA'ishah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ whether there would be any torment in the grave before the Day of Resurrection, and he ﷺ said, "No — who said that?" She told him it was the Jewish woman, and he ﷺ said, "The Jews are lying, and they tell more lies about Allah. There is no torment except on the Day of Resurrection." Then as much time passed as Allah willed should pass, and one day he came out at midday, wrapped in his robe, his eyes reddening, calling at the top of his voice: "The grave is like patches of dark night! O people, if you knew what I know, you would weep much and laugh little. O people, seek refuge with Allah from the torment of the grave, for the torment of the grave is real." Ibn Kathir says this chain of narration is Sahih according to the conditions of Al-Bukhari and Muslim, although they did not record it.

Ibn Kathir also cites a **separate** narration of **ʿA'ishah** recorded by **Imam Ahmad** — and also recorded by **Muslim** — in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon her while a Jewish woman was with her, and the woman was saying, "I was told that you will be tried in the grave." The Messenger of Allah was worried and said, "Only the Jews will be tested." ʿA'ishah said that several nights passed, and then he ﷺ said, "Verily you will be tested in the graves." She added that after that, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to seek refuge with Allah from the torment of the grave.

How does Ibn Kathir reconcile the Makkan ayah with this? He offers the answer with care rather than certainty. The ayah speaks of the **souls** of Pharaoh's people being exposed to the Fire morning and evening; it does not say that the pain will affect their bodies in the grave. So it may be that this has to do specifically with their souls, while any effect upon the bodies in al-Barzakh, and their feeling pain as a result, is what the Sunnah indicates separately, in hadiths he says are "very many." He also notes it was said that the ayah refers to the punishment of the disbelievers in al-Barzakh, and does not by itself imply that a believer will be punished in the grave for his sins. He observes that when Allah revealed something about the torment of the grave to His Prophet ﷺ, he sought refuge with Allah from that. And Ibn Kathir closes the discussion, as the scholars do when a matter is not decisively settled, with "And Allah knows best."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the doctrinal outcome plainly: this verse is a proof of punishment in the graves, and uninterrupted reports of ahadith together with the consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of the Muslim Ummah confirm it. Its author notes that he gathered the material on this subject, along with the relevant verses of the Qur'an, in a treatise entitled *As-sabr bi-ʿadhābi-l-qabr*, published in Arabic as part of *Ahkām-ul-Qur'ān*.

### The other side of the same barzakh

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān bring the hadith of **Ibn ʿUmar**, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Kathir records it from **Imam Ahmad** and notes it was also reported in the Two Sahihs; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it as appearing in the two Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim: "When one of you dies, he is shown his place morning and evening; if he is one of the people of Paradise, then he is one of the people of Paradise, and if he is one of the people of Hell, then he is one of the people of Hell. It will be said to him: this is your place until Allah resurrects you to go to it on the Day of Resurrection."

This is the mercy hidden inside the terror of ayah 46. The same daily showing that is rebuke and humiliation for Pharaoh's people is, for the believer, a daily glimpse of home. The man of ayah 44 who said "I entrust my affair to Allah" is, by ayah 45, on the other side of that showing.

## Living it

**Say the truth, then hand over the outcome.** The believer's final speech contains no plan for self-protection — only *ufawwiḍu amrī ilā Allāh*. He spoke, he expected harm, and he transferred the file to Allah. Ayah 45 is what happened next. This is the pattern for anyone who has to say something unwelcome and true, at cost.

**Invite the way he invited.** He named their position honestly ("you invite me to the Fire"), showed that it rested on nothing ("of which I have no knowledge"), and still held out the door — *al-ʿAzīz al-Ghaffār*, the Mighty who forgives whoever turns back to Him. Warning and hope in the same breath.

**Take the grave seriously.** In the narration Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, the Prophet ﷺ came out at midday with reddening eyes, calling out that the grave is like patches of dark night and telling his people to seek refuge with Allah from its torment. In a separate narration — recorded by Imam Ahmad and also by Muslim — ʿA'ishah says that after he ﷺ told them "you will be tested in the graves," he used to seek refuge with Allah from the torment of the grave. And ayah 46 says that for some, the account is already being read out twice a day. That should change how a believer spends a morning and an evening.

passages.title: The followers and the arrogant quarrel in Hell
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take us inside the Fire and let us listen. Two conversations are recorded: first the followers turn on the leaders they once obeyed (47–48), then those in the Fire turn to the angels who guard Hell (49–50). What holds the passage together is a single grim discovery — that on that Day there is no one left to lean on. Every source of help the disbelievers reach for is tried in turn, and every one of them comes back empty.

## Where we are standing

Ibn Kathir opens his comment simply: "Allah tells us how the people of Hell will dispute and argue with one another, and Fir'awn and his people will be among them." That last clause anchors the passage to what came just before it. Ayah 46 spoke of the Fire "before which they are presented morning and evening," and of the day when the Hour comes and the order is released: "Admit the family of the Pharaoh into the most severe punishment." So when ayah 47 says "when they will dispute in the Fire," we are watching that sentence carried out — and among the disputants are the very people the surah has been telling us about.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on that earlier ayah, because it opens a window on what happens between death and resurrection. Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) explained ayah 46 by saying that the spirits of people from the House of Pharaoh are presented before Jahannam in the form of black birds, twice every day, morning and evening, and Jahannam is pointed out to them with the words: *this is your abode.* (Reported by ʿAbd-ur-Razzāq and Ibn Abi Haim — Mazhari.)

And according to a narration of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) appearing in the two Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said, in meaning: when one of you dies — and is in the world of *barzakh*, the state after death and before resurrection — he is shown, morning and evening, the place he is to reach after the reckoning of the Day of Judgement. This place is shown to him every day, and he is told that he has to reach there finally: if he is of the people of Jannah, Jannah is shown to him as his place; if he is of the people of Jahannam, Jahannam is shown to him as his place.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the doctrinal conclusion plainly: this ayah is a proof of punishment in the grave, confirmed by uninterrupted reports of aḥādīth and by the consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of the Muslim Ummah. The author notes that he gathered all such material, along with the relevant verses of the Qur'an, in a treatise in Arabic, *As-Sabr bi-ʿadhāb al-qabr*, published as part of *Aḥkām al-Qur'ān*.

So the argument in ayat 47–50 does not fall on people who had no warning. The dispute we are about to overhear is what is said when a long-announced verdict finally lands.

## The first conversation: the followers and the leaders (47–48)

The scene opens with a dispute: "when they will dispute in the Fire." Ibn Kathir's heading for the whole passage is exactly that — "The Dispute of the People of Hell" — people arguing with one another after every argument has stopped mattering.

The two parties are named by what they were, not who they were. On one side "the weak," whom Ibn Kathir identifies as the followers. On the other "those who were arrogant," whom he identifies as "the leaders and masters." Notice that we are not given names. We are given positions — and anyone can find himself standing in one of them.

The weak open with an admission and then a request:

**"Verily, we followed you."** Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "we obeyed you and heeded your call to disbelief and misguidance in the world." That is the hinge of the whole exchange. They are not claiming they were dragged; they concede that they obeyed and heeded.

**"Can you then take from us some portion of the Fire?"** Ibn Kathir gives the sense: "can you carry a part of our burden for us?" It is worth sitting with how modest the request is. They are not asking to be released, and they are not asking to be saved. They are asking for *a portion* to be lifted — a share of the load carried by someone else.

The answer in ayah 48 comes back cold. **"We are all in it!"** Ibn Kathir renders their meaning: "we will not bear any part of your burden for you; our own punishment is enough for us to bear." Whatever these leaders once had in their hands, they have nothing left to give.

Then they add the line that closes the conversation for good: **"Verily, Allah has judged between His servants."** Ibn Kathir explains: "He has shared out the punishment among us according to what each of us deserves." This is the theological centre of the passage. The leaders are not appealing to fate or to bad luck. They are stating, correctly and too late, that the distribution of punishment is a matter of divine justice — measured out to each according to what he deserves, and now settled. No transfer, no bargain, no reallocation between parties.

Ibn Kathir adds that this is like the ayah in which Allah says: **"For each one there is double (torment), but you know not"** (7:38).

**What this asks of us.** The passage quietly dismantles the oldest excuse there is: *I was only following.* These people had that excuse ready and they used it — and it moved nothing. Nor does leadership shield the leader. Whoever we imitate now, whoever we let set our standards of belief and behaviour, may one day say to us with perfect honesty, *our own punishment is enough for us to bear.*

## The second conversation: the appeal to the keepers (49)

Having failed with each other, "those in the Fire" turn to the keepers of Hell — the angels set over it, whom Ibn Kathir describes as "like jailers watching over the people of Hell." Their plea is: **"Call upon your Lord to lighten for us the torment for a day!"**

Two things here are devastating once you see them.

First, notice whom they ask. Ibn Kathir explains why they turn to the angels at all: "They know that Allah will not answer them and will not listen to their prayer," because He has already said — and Ibn Kathir cites it — **"Remain you in it with ignominy! And speak you not to Me!"** (23:108). That is a door already closed in words. So they look for someone else to carry the request.

Second, notice how small the request has become. They do not ask for release, or for the Fire to be extinguished, or even for a permanent easing. Ibn Kathir puts it exactly: they ask the keepers "to pray to Allah to lessen the Fire for them if only for one day." Read the passage in order and you watch the asking shrink — from "carry a part of our burden" down to "one day, a little less." And even that is refused.

## The keepers' question and the final verdict (50)

The angels do not argue about whether the punishment is fair. They ask one question: **"Did there not come to you your Messengers with clear evidences?"** Ibn Kathir gives the force of it: "was not proof established in the world on the lips of the Messengers?" The translation of the ayah renders the question as whether the messengers did not *constantly* come to them — not one visit easily missed, but a message delivered again and again, and delivered with clear evidences.

The answer is a single word: **"Yes."** No dispute, no counter-argument, no plea of ignorance. The case for the punishment is closed by the mouths of the punished.

Then comes the sentence: **"Then call (as you like)!"** Ibn Kathir spells out everything packed into that dismissal: "you are on your own. We will not pray for you or listen to you; we do not want you to be saved and we have nothing to do with you. Moreover, we tell you that it is all the same whether you offer supplication or not, because Allah will not respond and He will not lighten the torment for you."

The keepers close with a general truth, and the passage ends on it: **"And the invocation of the disbelievers is nothing but in vain."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and final: "it will not be accepted or responded to."

## What the passage leaves us with

Read as a whole, ayat 47–50 walk through every source of help a person might reach for and show each one empty in turn:

- **The people you followed** (47–48) — they will not bear any part of your burden; their own punishment is enough for them to bear.
- **A collective bargain** — there is none, because "Allah has judged between His servants," the punishment shared out according to what each deserves.
- **Someone with access to put in a word** (49) — the keepers will not pray for them and do not want them saved.
- **Your own supplication** (50) — the invocation of the disbelievers "will not be accepted or responded to."

That last point is the one to feel. What Ibn Kathir describes is not duʿāʾ failing in itself; it is duʿāʾ failing *there*, for those who were given clear evidences again and again and turned away. Today those doors are open. The Messengers came with clear evidences; the invitation stands; and the angels' question — "did there not come to you your Messengers with clear evidences?" — is one whose answer we are still writing.

passages.title: Allah's help for His messengers and Moses' legacy
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Allah's guarantee to the ones who carry His message: His messengers and those who believe with them will be helped — in this world and on the Day the witnesses rise to testify. Ayat 51–52 state the promise and then show the other side of it, the collapse of the wrongdoers' case on that Day. Ayat 53–54 supply the historical proof: Musa was given guidance, and his people ended up inheriting both the land and the Book. Ayah 55 turns the whole thing into instructions for the Prophet ﷺ himself — be patient, seek forgiveness, and glorify your Lord morning and evening. The thread running through all five is one idea: the outcome is already settled, so live now in the manner of someone who knows that.

## The promise, and how it is worded

Look at how heavily ayah 51 is stressed. Every rendering of it in our sources reaches for an intensifier — "We certainly help," "Verily, We will indeed make victorious," "Surely, We do help." This is not offered as a hope or as a general principle. It is stated as a promise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as a standing promise rather than a one-time rescue: the verse "carries the promise of Allah Taʿala that He would keep helping His messengers and believers, both in the present world and in the Hereafter." Not one deliverance at one moment in history — a continuing way of Allah with His messengers.

And Maʿārif adds the obvious point that we should not skip past: "It is obvious that this help is intended to be against adversaries and enemies." The help promised here is not vague comfort. It is help *against* someone.

One more thing worth noticing: the promise is not restricted to the messengers. It says "and those who believe." Ordinary believers are folded into the same guarantee as prophets. Whoever stands with the message stands inside the promise.

## The honest objection — and the answer

Here is where this passage becomes genuinely deep, because Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to pretend the difficulty is not there.

If Allah always helps His messengers against their enemies, what do we make of the prophets who were killed, or who had to flee? Maʿārif names them: Sayyidna Yahya, Zakariyya and Shuʿaib (peace be upon them), "who were either martyred by enemies or had to abandon their home country and migrate to some other place — as was the case with Sayyidna Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and the last of the prophets, Sayyidna Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ." Maʿārif then says plainly: "There may be some doubt about that."

That is a serious question, and it is the question a believer under pressure actually asks.

The answer, which Maʿārif takes from Ibn Kathir citing Ibn Jarir, turns on a single word. The verse says *nusrah* — help. And *nusrah* here is being used in the sense of *intisar*: victory, the subduing of the enemy in retaliation. Crucially, that subduing may come "at their hands while they are alive, or after their death." Once you read the promise that way, Maʿārif notes, "this meaning applies to all prophets and believers without any exception."

As-Suddi, quoted by Ibn Kathir, says the same thing from the other end. Allah never sends a messenger to a people, and they kill him or kill some of the believers who call them to the truth, and that generation passes away, except that He then sends them someone who will support their call and seek vengeance for their blood from those who did that to them — in this world. As-Suddi's conclusion is the sentence to hold on to: **"So the Prophets and believers may be killed in this world, but their call will prevail in this world."**

That is the shape of the divine promise. It does not guarantee that the individual will survive. It guarantees that the message will win and the persecutors will not get away with it.

Maʿārif then walks through the record, because it says history bears witness. Those who killed Sayyidna Yahya, Zakariyya and Shuʿaib (peace be upon them) had enemies set loose upon them "who showed no mercy while disgracing and killing them." As for Namrud (Nimrod), terrible was the punishment that overtook him. Against the enemies of Sayyidna ʿIsa (peace be upon him), Allah set the power of Byzantium, which defeated and disgraced them — and Maʿārif adds that Allah will give him ascendancy over his enemies close to the Last Day. In every case the vindication came. Sometimes it came long after the funeral.

## The promise as it played out for the Prophet ﷺ

Ibn Kathir tells the story of ayah 51 in the life of the Prophet ﷺ almost as a single breath, and it is worth following the sequence, because each step is a piece of the promise being paid out.

Allah gave victory to His Prophet ﷺ and his Companions over those who had opposed him, disbelieved in him and shown hostility towards him, and He caused His Word and His religion to prevail over all other religions. He commanded him to emigrate from his people to Al-Madinah, and there He gave him supporters and helpers. Then He caused him to prevail over the idolaters on the day of Badr — their leaders killed, their elite taken prisoner and driven before him in chains — and then the Prophet ﷺ did them the favour of accepting ransom from them. Shortly afterwards Allah enabled him to conquer Makkah, and he rejoiced in returning to his homeland, the sacred and holy land of Al-Haram, which Allah saved through him from its disbelief and shirk. Then Yemen was opened to him, the entire Arabian Peninsula submitted, and the people entered the religion of Allah in crowds.

Then, Ibn Kathir says, Allah took him in death "because of his high status and honor," and established his Companions as his Khalifahs. They carried the religion onward from him, called mankind to Allah, conquered region after region and city after city, and opened people's hearts, "until the call of Muhammad ﷺ spread throughout the world, east and west. This religion will continue to prevail until the Hour begins."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same account with one detail highlighted: the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ were made to stand subdued at the hands of the Muslims themselves — their arrogant chiefs killed, some taken prisoner — and when the rest were rounded up at the conquest of Makkah, "the Holy Prophet ﷺ let them have their freedom." The victory the verse promises did not have to end in vengeance to count as victory. His message spread all over; the faith prevailed; the state of Islam stood established across the entire Arabian Peninsula within his lifetime — and the men who had opposed him were released.

## The Day the witnesses stand

Ayah 51 gives the promise two arenas: this world's life, and "the Day when the witnesses will stand forth." Ibn Kathir comments that on the Day of Resurrection "the victory will be greater and more complete." Worldly vindication is real, but partial; that Day is where it is finished.

Who are these witnesses? Mujahid said: "The witnesses are the angels." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the phrase means the day of Qiyamah, and that once the witnesses are standing to give their testimony, "Divine help for prophets and believers will show itself specially."

There is a point about the wording here that Ibn Kathir raises. Ayah 52, "the Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers," is referring to the same Day as "the Day when the witnesses will stand forth" in ayah 51 — the second phrase names the first one over again. Ibn Kathir notes that others read the two together with that same meaning: "And the Day the witnesses will stand forth, is a Day when there will be no profit to wrongdoers." Either way, the effect is the same. The Day of testimony *is* the day excuses die. Where there are witnesses, there is no room left for a story.

## Ayah 52: three things taken away

Ibn Kathir identifies the wrongdoers here as the idolaters, and then unpacks the three clauses of the verse in turn.

**Their excuses will not profit them.** Ibn Kathir's gloss widens the loss: it means "no excuse or ransom will be accepted from them." Not the argument, not the payment. Both routes out are closed. Remember that just above, the Prophet ﷺ had *accepted* ransom for the prisoners of Badr. In this world, ransom worked. On that Day it does not.

**Theirs will be the curse.** This, Ibn Kathir explains, means "they will be cast out far away from the mercy of Allah." Not abuse — distance. To be under this curse is to be removed from the reach of the mercy.

**Theirs will be the evil abode.** Ibn Kathir says this is the Hell-fire, and quotes As-Suddi: "a terrible abode and dwellingplace." Note the words *abode* and *dwellingplace* — the place you settle, not the place you pass through.

## Musa: the promise already in the record (53–54)

Ibn Kathir titles this section precisely: an "Indication that the Messenger and the Believers will prevail just as Musa and the Children of Israel prevailed." Ayah 53 is not a change of subject. It is the evidence exhibit for ayah 51.

"And, indeed We gave Musa the guidance" — Ibn Kathir explains this as the guidance and light with which Allah sent him. That is what a messenger is given first: not an army, but guidance.

"And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture." Ibn Kathir reads the inheritance in the fullest sense: "We caused them to prevail in the end and they inherited the land and accumulated wealth of Firʿawn." A community that had been under the tyrant ended up holding his territory and his treasure. That is ayah 51 in concrete form.

And then Ibn Kathir names the reason — this is the line that makes 53 a lesson rather than a story: they inherited all of it **"because of their patience in obeying Allah and following His Messenger Musa."** Patience in obedience, and loyalty to the messenger. That is the price of admission to the promise, and it explains why the very next command in ayah 55 is "So be patient."

The Scripture they inherited, Ibn Kathir says, was the Tawrah, and ayah 54 describes it: "a guide and a reminder for men of understanding." Both words are needed, and they do different work: a guide is for the one who does not yet know the way, a reminder for the one who knows and forgets. Ibn Kathir glosses "men of understanding" as those "of a sound and upright nature." Which quietly suggests something important: being guided by revelation turns on the soundness of a person's nature, not merely on the sharpness of his mind.

## Ayah 55: what the promise asks of you

Everything now turns into three imperatives addressed to the Prophet ﷺ.

**"So be patient."** Ibn Kathir supplies the addressee: "O Muhammad." And notice the "So" — the command follows from everything said before it. Because the promise is what it is, and because Musa's people inherited by patience — be patient.

**"Verily, the promise of Allah is true."** Ibn Kathir renders the meaning as Allah addressing His Prophet ﷺ directly: We have promised that your word will prevail and that the ultimate victory will be for you and those who follow you, and Allah does not break His promises; what We have told you is true, and there is no doubt in it whatsoever. This is the ground the patience stands on. Sabr here is not gritted teeth in an uncertain situation. It is composure in a situation whose ending has already been announced by the One who does not break His promises.

**"And ask forgiveness for your fault."** Of this Ibn Kathir says one short sentence: "This encourages the Ummah to seek forgiveness." Notice where the command lands. In a passage about victory over enemies, the Prophet ﷺ — the one being promised the victory — is told to seek forgiveness. The message reaching the community is unmistakable: if he is told to do this, no one below him has an excuse to skip it.

**"And glorify the praises of your Lord in the ʿAshi and the Ibkar."** Ibn Kathir defines the two windows: *al-ʿAshi* is "the end of the day and the beginning of the night," and *al-Ibkar* is "the beginning of the day and the end of the night." So the two seams of the day — the fading of light into dark, and the lifting of dark into light — are the appointed times for praising your Lord. Two hinges, one at each end, holding the day in place.

## Living it

Put the pieces together and this passage gives a believer a settled posture rather than a mood.

**Redefine what winning looks like.** As-Suddi's line reframes everything: the messengers and believers may be killed, but their call will prevail. If you measure the promise of ayah 51 by whether righteous people are personally spared, you will be confused by history. Measure it by whether the truth ends up standing and the oppressor ends up answering for what he did, and the promise holds without exception — sometimes at their hands while they are alive, sometimes, as Ibn Jarir's answer allows, only after their death.

**Patience is the qualification.** The Children of Israel inherited land, wealth and Scripture because of patience in obeying Allah and following His Messenger Musa. That is the mechanism, stated plainly by Ibn Kathir. The promise is not delivered to the impatient.

**Handle your account now.** Ayah 52 shows a moment when excuses and ransom are both refused. Ayah 55 shows the alternative while it is still open: seeking forgiveness. Istighfar in this world is the substitute for the excuse that will not be accepted in the Hereafter.

**Anchor the day at both ends.** The passage does not close with strategy or with a call to arms. It closes with the praise of your Lord at dusk and at dawn. That is what a person does while waiting for a promise that is certain but not yet visible — patience, seeking forgiveness, and glorifying his Lord at the two ends of every day.

passages.title: Arrogant disputers and the certainty of the Hour
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the promise of victory given to the Prophet ﷺ to the inner condition of the people who fight that victory — and then to the two truths their pride is refusing: that the One who made the heavens can certainly raise the dead, and that the Hour is coming whether or not anyone believes in it. What binds the passage into one unit is a single diagnosis given in ayah 56: the dispute is not really about evidence at all. It is about pride. Once that is seen, the argument of ayah 57, the contrast of ayah 58, and the flat certainty of ayah 59 all read as answers to a disease of the heart rather than as moves in a debate.

## Where the passage is standing

Just before this, Allah promises that He will make His Messengers and the believers victorious "in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth." Mujahid said the witnesses are the angels, and Ibn Kathir notes that on the Day of Resurrection "the victory will be greater and more complete."

Ibn Kathir unfolds that promise historically. Allah granted victory to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions over those who had opposed him, disbelieved in him and shown hostility towards him; He commanded him to emigrate to Al-Madinah, where He gave him supporters and helpers; then He caused him to prevail over the idolators on the day of Badr; then Allah enabled him to conquer Makkah, and "he rejoiced in his return to his homeland, the sacred and holy land of Al-Haram"; then the Yemen, "and the entire Arabian Peninsula submitted to him, and the people entered the religion of Allah in crowds." After Allah took him in death, his Companions carried the religion from him and called mankind to Allah, "until the call of Muhammad ﷺ spread throughout the world, east and west. This religion will continue to prevail until the Hour begins."

As-Suddi's observation sits underneath it. Allah never sends a Messenger to a people who kill him or some of the believers who call them to the truth, and that generation passes away, but that He then sends someone who will support their call and seek vengeance for their blood from those who did that to them in this world. "So the Prophets and believers may be killed in this world, but their call will prevail in this world."

Then Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that He gave Musa the guidance — "the guidance and light with which Allah sent him" — and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture, which Ibn Kathir explains as: "We caused them to prevail in the end and they inherited the land and accumulated wealth of Firʿawn, because of their patience in obeying Allah and following His Messenger Musa."

And then the instruction: **be patient**, for the promise of Allah is true — Ibn Kathir paraphrases it as Allah saying that the ultimate victory will be for the Prophet ﷺ and those who follow him, "and Allah does not break His promises"; **ask forgiveness**, which Ibn Kathir says "encourages the Ummah to seek forgiveness"; and **glorify the praises of your Lord in the ʿAshī and the Ibkār** — which Ibn Kathir explains as the end of the day and the beginning of the night, and the beginning of the day and the end of the night.

So ayah 56 arrives to a man who has just been told to be patient. It tells him what kind of opponent he is being patient with.

## Ayah 56: disputing with nothing in hand

"Surely those who dispute Allah's signs — with no proof given to them…" Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "without any authority having come to them," and his gloss is precise: "they try to refute the truth with falsehood, and to refute sound evidence with dubious arguments, having no proof or evidence from Allah."

Notice the shape of that. It is not that they hold a rival body of evidence. They meet clear proof with murk. They do not out-argue the revelation; they cloud it, so that a listener who was on the edge of accepting loses his footing. That is a recognisable move in every age. Someone who cannot answer a truth can still make it feel doubtful, and to a person who wants an excuse, doubt is as good as a refutation.

## What is actually in the chest

Then the Qur'an does something remarkable: it goes past the argument and names the motive. **"There is nothing else in their breasts except pride. They will never have it."**

Ibn Kathir: "they are too proud to follow the truth and submit to the one who has brought it." Both halves matter. Some hearts could accept the truth in the abstract but cannot bear the specific humiliation of taking it from *this* man — of standing behind someone they had placed beneath themselves. Notice that Ibn Kathir does not say only that they refused to *believe* the truth; he says they were too proud to *follow* it and to *submit* to the one who brought it. Following requires you to step down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, opens this out in a way worth sitting with. Those who quarrel about the verses of Allah without any valid argument, it says, "really look forward to rejecting this faith simply because their hearts are filled with pride and arrogance." They "would like to stay ahead in the game and are so dim-witted that they have taken for granted that they have this position of strength as a result of their staunch adherence to their faith, and if they were to surrender this stance by becoming Muslims, they will be left without any power and territory of their own." It is worth understanding why that description is fair rather than merely harsh. They had made a calculation about where honour comes from, and the calculation was simply wrong.

## "They will never reach it"

That is what the closing phrase of the clause answers: *mā hum bi-bālighīh* — "they are not able to reach it." Two readings run together here and both are in the sources.

Ibn Kathir reads it as the failure of the project: "their attempts to suppress the truth and elevate falsehood will fail; the truth will prevail and their words and aspirations will be defeated." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as the failure of the ambition itself: "these people will never reach the goals of their assumed pride, greatness and state power without embracing Islam." And then the sentence that turns the whole thing inside out — "however, had they embraced Islam, honour and greatness would have followed in their footsteps."

That is the cruel logic of this pride. They refused submission in order to protect their greatness, and refusing submission was precisely what forfeited it. The thing they were clutching would have been given to them had they opened their hands. Set this against Ibn Kathir's account of what happened next — Badr, Makkah, the Yemen, the Peninsula, then east and west — and you can see the promise and the warning meeting in history.

## The refuge at the end of the ayah

The ayah ends with a command that lands on the believer, not on the disputer: "So seek refuge in Allah. Verily, it is He Who is the All-Hearer, the All-Seer."

Ibn Kathir is careful about what the refuge is *from*. It means seeking refuge with Allah "from being like these people" — "from being like these people who dispute about the Ayat of Allah without any authority having come to them." This is the passage's sharpest turn. You might expect: seek refuge from their harm. Instead: seek refuge from their *condition*. A man can begin defending the truth and end up defending himself.

And the ayah seals that command with two of Allah's names: **the All-Hearer** and **the All-Seer**. Whatever else a dispute is, it is conducted in front of the One who hears it and sees it.

## Ayah 57: the greater and the lesser

"The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind; yet, most of the people do not know."

Ibn Kathir titles this section **Life after Death**, because this is an argument for the resurrection. Allah tells us that He will bring back His creation on the Day of Resurrection, and "that is very easy for Him, because He created the heavens and the earth, and creating them is greater than creating mankind, the first time and when He creates them again. The One Who is able to do that is able to do anything that is less than that." He brings the parallel verse: "Do they not see that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, He surely is able to do all things" (46:33).

The reasoning moves from the greater to the lesser, and its force depends on something the objectors already conceded. Ibn Kathir points this out with real edge: "many of the Arabs recognized that Allah had created the heavens and the earth, but they denied and rejected the idea of the resurrection; they acknowledged something which was greater than that which they denied." They had already admitted the harder case and were baulking at the easier one.

Which is why the ayah closes not with "they do not accept" but with **"most of the people do not know."** Ibn Kathir: "hence they do not think about or ponder this proof." The evidence is not hidden. The sky is over their heads. What is missing is the act of turning the mind onto it — and this connects straight back to ayah 56, because a chest full of pride is not a chest that reflects. Pride does not usually argue its way out of a proof; it simply declines to look at it.

## Ayah 58: two men, one road

"And not equal are the blind and those who see; nor are those who believe, and do righteous good deeds, and those who do evil. Little do you remember!"

Ibn Kathir keeps the image concrete before drawing the lesson: "The blind man who cannot see anything is not the same as the sighted man who can see everything as far as his eyesight reaches — there is a huge difference between them. By the same token, the righteous believers and the immoral disbelievers are not equal."

The comparison is doing a specific job in this passage. Ayah 57 has just said the failure is one of *knowing* and of *pondering*; ayah 58 gives that failure its picture. The disputer is not a rival observer reporting a different landscape. He is a man with his eyes shut describing the road.

Two details are easy to pass over. First, faith is paired with **righteous deeds** — "those who believe, and do righteous good deeds." Sight, in this comparison, is not a claim held in the mind; it is a life that moves correctly because it can see where it is going. Second, the ayah does not close with a threat but with a sigh: *qalīlan mā tatadhakkarūn* — "little do you remember." Ibn Kathir's gloss is quietly devastating: "most of the people remember little." Not *know* little — **remember** little. The material for reflection has already been given. It is lying unused.

## Ayah 59: the Hour, with or without you

"Verily, the Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it, yet most men believe not."

Ibn Kathir's comment on the first clause is deliberately plain: it "means, it will indeed come to pass." There is no fresh argument in this ayah, because after ayah 57 no argument is owed. The One who built the heavens is not strained by raising the dead; therefore the Hour is not a possibility to be weighed but a fact to be met.

*Lā rayba fīhā* — "there is no doubt about it." The Qur'an declares that the Hour holds no doubt in it at all, and then, in the same breath, reports that most people do not believe. The doubt was never in the matter. It was only ever in them. Ibn Kathir puts it starkly: "they do not believe in it, and in fact they doubt its existence altogether."

And there is the passage's final irony. Three times across these ayat the majority is invoked — *most of the people do not know* (57), *little do you remember* (58), *most men believe not* (59). Numbers settle nothing. The Hour is not waiting for a consensus.

## Living it
