**Watch what an argument is for.** Ayah 56 says that a dispute can be entirely about evidence on the surface and entirely about pride underneath. Before entering one, ask what would happen inside you if the other person turned out to be right. If the answer is that something in you would be unbearably diminished, then the disease the ayah names is already in the room, and Ibn Kathir has told you what to do about it: seek refuge in Allah from being like those people.

**Do not defend a position because of what you have invested in it.** That is precisely the trap Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes: they assumed their position of strength rested on holding their ground, when in truth, "had they embraced Islam, honour and greatness would have followed in their footsteps." What we fear losing by yielding to the truth is very often the thing yielding would have given us.

**Use the proof that is already in front of you.** Ayah 57's whole complaint, in Ibn Kathir's words, is that people "do not think about or ponder this proof." The heavens are the argument, and looking up with a thinking heart is not a spare-time luxury.

**Take the pairing in ayah 58 seriously.** Belief and righteous action are named together. Sight that changes nothing about how a person walks is not the sight the ayah is praising.

**And live as though ayah 59 were true, because it is.** The command given to the Prophet ﷺ just before this passage points the way: be patient, for the promise of Allah is true; ask forgiveness — and that command, Ibn Kathir says, "encourages the Ummah to seek forgiveness"; and glorify the praises of your Lord at the close of the day and at its opening. The disputers of ayah 56 spent their certainty on a greatness they never reached. The believer spends his on a Day that is certainly coming.

passages.title: Call upon Me: the Ever-Living Lord and His signs
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are one continuous invitation. Allah opens with an astonishing offer — **"Call upon Me, I will respond to you"** (ayah 60) — and then spends four ayat showing you exactly *who* it is you would be calling: the One who gives you night and day, who spread out the earth and raised the sky, who shaped your very body and put good food on your table. Ayah 65 closes the circle by repeating the same command with one added condition: **"so call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His."** It begins with *adʿūnī* ("call Me") and ends with *fa-dʿūhu* ("so call Him"). Everything in between is the reason.

## "Call upon Me, I will respond to you"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *duʿāʼ* literally means **to call**, and is most often used for calling out for something you need. Sometimes *dhikr* — the acts devoted to remembering Allah — is itself called *duʿāʼ*.

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line of pure warmth: by His grace and kindness, Allah *encourages* His servants to call upon Him, and He *guarantees* to respond.

Ibn Kathir reports that Sufyān ath-Thawrī used to say: "O You Who love most those who ask of You, and O You Who hate most those who do not ask of You, and there is no one like that apart from You, O Lord." (Recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim.) And a poet put the same point in one line: "Allah hates not to be asked, and the son of Adam hates to be asked."

**A privilege given to this Ummah.** Ibn Kathir records from Qatādah, from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, that this community has been given three things given to no nation before it — things previously said only to Prophets. When Allah sent a Prophet, He said to him, "You are a witness over your nation"; but this Ummah was made witnesses over mankind. It was said to Prophets individually that Allah had not laid upon them any hardship in religion, but He said it to this entire Ummah (22:78). And it was said to the Prophets individually, *"Call upon Me, I will answer you"* — and now it is said to all of us: **ادْعُونِي أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ**. (Recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: this ayah confers a special honour on the followers of the Prophet ﷺ, ordering them to make duʿāʼ with the assurance that it would be answered. What was once peculiar to Prophets has been universalised.

## Duʿāʼ *is* worship

The second half of ayah 60 does something unexpected. Allah says the threat is for **"those who show arrogance against worshipping Me"** — but the thing they scorned, in the first half of the ayah, was *calling upon Him*. Allah has quietly equated the two.

The Prophet ﷺ made the equation explicit. Imam Ahmad recorded from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **إِنَّ الدُّعَاءَ هُوَ الْعِبَادَةُ** — *"Indeed, supplication is worship."* He then recited this very ayah. Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by the Sunan compilers — at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʼī, Ibn Mājah — as well as Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarīr; at-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." It was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʼī and Ibn Jarīr through a different chain.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something subtle here from Tafsīr Maẓharī. In Arabic, a sentence of this construction confines the predicate to the subject — so the hadith can mean: *every duʿāʼ is worship.* But reverse the same rule and it can also mean: *every act of worship is duʿāʼ.* Duʿāʼ and *ʿibādah* are separate in their literal senses, yet unified in substance: different words, one substance.

Why? Because *ʿibādah* is essentially the posture of showing one's utter modesty and abasement before someone — and extending your hand before Him like a beggar with his bowl *is* that posture, exactly. And in the other direction: the outcome of every act of worship is to ask Allah for forgiveness, for Paradise, and for a perfect state of well-being in this world and the next. Every prayer you pray is already a request.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two supports. In a ḥadīth qudsī — a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ conveys a saying from Allah that is not part of the Qur'an — Allah said: "One who is so engrossed in remembering Me that he does not have even the time to ask for what he needs, I shall give him more than those who ask" (reported by al-Jazrī in *An-Nihāyah*). And in a narration appearing in Tirmidhī and Muslim, the wording is: "One who is so engrossed in the recitation of the Qur'an that he does not have even the time to ask for what he needs, I shall give him even more than what those who ask ever get." So every act of worship brings the same benefit as duʿāʼ.

And in the ḥadīth of ʿArafāt, the Prophet ﷺ said that his duʿāʼ at ʿArafāt, and that of the Prophets before him, was: *lā ilāha illa'llāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lahu, lahu'l-mulku wa lahu'l-ḥamdu wa huwa ʿalā kulli shayʼin qadīr* — "There is no god but Allah who is one. No one shares His godhead. To Him belongs the kingdom and to Him belongs all praise, and He is powerful over everything" (reported by Ibn Abi Shaibah — Maẓharī). That is pure praise, containing no request at all — and the Prophet ﷺ called it *duʿāʼ*.

## Who exactly is being warned

Read the threat carefully: **"those who show arrogance against worshipping Me shall enter Jahannam, disgraced."** The condition is not *not asking*; it is **arrogance**. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as "those who are too proud to call on Me and single Me out."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise about the ruling. The warning of Jahannam applies to the person who, in his pride, considers himself in no need of making duʿāʼ and actually abandons it — and that attitude is a sign of *kufr* (open infidelity), so the warning became due against him. Otherwise, making duʿāʼ as such is not *farḍ* (obligatory) or *wājib* (necessary); leaving it off brings no sin. By the consensus of the scholars it is *mustaḥabb* (recommended) and *afḍal* (better, meritworthy), and in accordance with clarifications in the ahadith, it is a source of much *barakah* (blessing). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Tafsīr Maẓharī, after gathering the narrations on divine wrath towards one who does not ask, applies them specifically to the one whose abstention is based on arrogance and on taking oneself to be free of need.

There is a fitting justice in the punishment. Ibn Kathir explains **دَاخِرِينَ** (*dākhirīn*) as entering "in disgrace and insignificance." Those who thought themselves too big to lower their hands are made small. Ibn Kathir cites Imam Ahmad's report from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The proud will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like ants in the image of people, and everything will be stepping on them, humiliating them, until they enter a prison in Hell called Būlas. They will be fed flames of fire, and given for drink a paste of insanity dripping from the people of the Fire."

**The merits of duʿāʼ**, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers them:

- "There is nothing more deserving of regard by Allah than duʿāʼ" — Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and Ḥākim, from Abū Hurayrah.
- "Duʿāʼ is the essence of ʿibādah" — Tirmidhī, from Anas ibn Mālik.
- "Ask Allah of His grace, because Allah likes being asked, and it is a great act of ʿibādah that one waits for ease while in hardship" — Tirmidhī, from Ibn Masʿūd.
- "Do not be weary of duʿāʼ, for nobody dies of making duʿāʼ" — Ibn Ḥibbān and Ḥākim, from Anas ibn Mālik.
- "Duʿāʼ is a weapon of the believer, a pillar of the faith, and the light of the heavens and the earth" — Ḥākim in *al-Mustadrak*, from Abū Hurayrah.
- "If the gates of duʿāʼ are opened for someone, the doors of mercy are opened for him; and no duʿāʼ made before Allah is appreciated more than that in which one asks Him for *ʿāfiyah*" — Tirmidhī and Ḥākim, from Ibn ʿUmar.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on that last word. **ʿĀfiyah** is a very comprehensive word — usually rendered "well-being," a state of being healthy and happy. Beyond a good life it takes in security from unwelcome happenings, trials and calamities, as well as the satisfactory fulfilment of all needs in life. If you do not know what to ask for, ask for that.

## "But my duʿāʼ was not answered"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers with a hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that whatever a Muslim prays for before Allah, He would let him have it — subject to the condition that the request is not for something sinful or for the severance of relationships Allah has enjoined be kept intact — and that the acceptance takes one of three forms: **(1)** one gets exactly what one asked for; **(2)** in lieu of what one wanted, one is given a certain return or reward in the Hereafter; **(3)** one does not get what one wanted, but some hardship or calamity that was due to fall on one stands removed. (Musnad Aḥmad — Maẓharī.) So no duʿāʼ is ever spent. It is only ever converted.

**A ruling.** Making duʿāʼ for committing a sin, or for the severance of blood relationships, is *ḥarām* (forbidden) — and such a duʿāʼ does not get to be accepted with Allah either, as in the hadith from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī.

**Conditions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes how open the ayah is: it obviously seems to have no condition, almost to the extent that even being a Muslim is not a condition — Allah accepts the duʿāʼ of a disbeliever too in this world, to the extent that the request of Iblīs to be allowed to live until the Day of Qiyāmah was accepted. There is no condition of a particular time, nor of being in a state of *ṭahārah* (purity from pollutants) or having performed *wuḍūʼ* (ablution). But there are trustworthy ahadith that identify a few things which preclude the chances of acceptance, and these are to be avoided. It is reported from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ described a man long on a journey, all dishevelled and dust-coated, stretching his hands upwards crying "O my Lord! O my Lord!" — while his food is unlawful, his drink unlawful, his dress unlawful, and he himself was brought up on the unlawful — "how then could his duʿāʼ become worth accepting?" (Reported by Muslim.) And words of duʿāʼ said negligently, heedlessly, without paying any attention, are likewise not accepted (Tirmidhī, from Abū Hurayrah).

## The signs: night, day, earth, sky, and yourself (61–64)

Ibn Kathir sums up ayah 61: Allah reminds us of His grace towards His creation in giving them **the night**, in which they rest and relax from their activities so that they can go back to them for their livelihood during the day, and **the day** with its light, in which they undertake their journeys and engage in their business. Then: *"Truly, Allah is full of bounty to mankind; yet most of mankind give no thanks"* — that is, Ibn Kathir says, they do not express gratitude for the favours which Allah bestows upon them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers here. Consider what a great blessing it is that all human beings — even animals — have been naturally tuned to a set time for sleep. It was made part of everyone's psyche that *this* time, the time of night, is what brings sound sleep. Otherwise, had sleep been in one's own control, with everyone making their own programme to sleep at different hours the way they set a timetable for business, it would have left all sleepers deprived of the bliss of sleep, nor would it have been convenient for those awake to set their own hours of work right — because human needs are inter-related. Had sleeping hours differed, the jobs of the awake connected with the sleeping, and of the sleeping connected with the awake, would have gone topsy-turvy. And even if only human beings had a set time for sleep, with wild beasts and animals sleeping at some other time, even then the system of human engagement with work would have gone haywire.

**The pivot (ayah 62).** *"That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no deity worthy of worship except Him."* Ibn Kathir: the One who does all of these things is Allah, the One, the Unique, the Creator of all things, besides whom there is no other god or lord. Then: *"How then are you turning away?"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, how can you worship idols which cannot create anything but are themselves hand-made and carved?

**Ayah 63** widens the lens: *"Thus were turned away those who used to deny the signs of Allah."* Ibn Kathir explains that just as these people — the Quraysh — were led astray by their worship of gods other than Allah, so those who came before them also disbelieved and worshipped others, with no proof or evidence, but on the basis of ignorance and desires.

**Ayah 64** turns from the sky to your own skin. Ibn Kathir on each phrase:
- *"made for you the earth a dwelling place"* — He made it stable and spread it out for you so that you might live on it and travel about in it, and He strengthened it with the mountains so that it does not shake with you.
- *"and the sky a canopy"* — a roof covering and protecting the world.
- *"and shaped you and made your shapes good"* — He created you in the best and most perfect form.
- *"and provided you with good and pure things"* — of food and drink in this world.

Ibn Kathir's summary is the whole argument in one sentence: Allah is the Creator of the dwelling place, of the inhabitants, and of the provision — He is the Creator and Provider. He links it to Sūrat al-Baqarah, where the identical logic ends in a command: *"O mankind, worship your Lord who created you… who made the earth a resting place for you and the sky as a canopy… then do not set up rivals unto Allah while you know"* (2:21–22).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out *"and shaped you, and made your shapes so good."* Allah has blessed the human person with the most distinct, superior and better-balanced form and shape out of all animals. He was given reason. He was given such hands and feet that he could gather materials to make things for his needs and comfort. Even his eating is a different order of thing: common animals eat or graze or drink directly with the mouth, and they eat singles — some meat, others grass or leaves. Man eats with his hands, and combines: meat, vegetables, spices, herbs and fruits, taking a single fruit from nature and turning it into pies, fruit cakes, jams, preserves and chutneys. Hence the ayah's own response: **فَتَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ** — Ibn Kathir renders the sense as: exalted and sanctified and glorified be Allah, the Lord of all the worlds.

## "He is the Ever-Living" (65)

**هُوَ الْحَيُّ** — *He is al-Ḥayy, the Ever-Living.* Ibn Kathir explains: He is the Ever-Living, from eternity to eternity, who was, is and shall be, the First and the Last, the Manifest, the Hidden. And *lā ilāha illā Huwa* — there is none comparable or equal to Him. Ayah 60 opened the door; ayah 65 tells you Who is on the other side of it.

Then the command returns, with its condition: **فَادْعُوهُ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ** — *"so call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His."* Ibn Kathir: this means affirming His Oneness by testifying that there is no god but He. Sincerity here is His oneness put into practice: the call goes to Him alone. And the ayah closes as the passage's argument must: *"All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all the worlds."*

Ibn Kathir attaches a practice to this ayah. Imam Ahmad recorded that after ending every prayer, ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr used to say: *"There is no true god except Allah alone, with no partner or associate; to Him belongs the dominion and the praise, for He is able to do all things. There is no strength and no power except with Allah. There is no true god except Allah, and we worship none but Him. To Him belong blessings and virtue and goodly praise. There is no true god except Allah — **we worship Him in all sincerity** (*mukhliṣīna lahu'd-dīn*) even though the disbelievers may hate that."* He said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say the *tahlīl* — the declaration *lā ilāha illā Allāh* — in this fashion after every prayer. Ibn Kathir notes that similar was also recorded by Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and an-Nasāʼī. The very phrase of ayah 65 sits inside that dhikr, placed on the tongue after every ṣalāh.

## Living it

- **Ask.** Not because Allah needs informing, but because asking is itself the worship He commanded, and He has guaranteed to respond. Refusing out of self-sufficiency is arrogance.
- **Ask for ʿāfiyah** when you cannot think what to ask.
- **Do not measure acceptance by delivery.** By the hadith Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites, your request returns to you as the thing itself, as reward stored up for the Hereafter, or as a calamity quietly removed.
- **Guard your intake and your attention.** Unlawful earnings and heedless words are the two obstacles the ahadith name.
- **Let the ordinary become evidence.** Tonight's sleep, tomorrow's daylight, the ground that does not shake, the roof of sky, your own hands, your dinner — ayat 61 to 64 train you to read these as signs rather than furniture. Most people, the ayah says, give no thanks.
- **Keep the call undivided.** *Mukhliṣīna lahu'd-dīn*: one Lord, one door, one direction.

passages.title: Worship none but the One who creates and gives life
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

These three ayat are a single argument. Ayah 66 is the refusal: the Prophet ﷺ is told to announce publicly that he has been forbidden to worship what the idolaters worship, and commanded instead to submit to the Lord of all that exists. Ayat 67 and 68 are the proof of that refusal — and the proof is not drawn from books or from the sky, but from the body of the person being addressed. Ibn Kathir titles the whole unit exactly this way: **the prohibition of shirk, the order for tawhid, and the evidence** — that is, the ban on giving worship to anything alongside Allah, the command to give it to Him alone, and then the reason why.

So the passage moves: *I will not worship them* → *here is why* → *and here is the reach of the One who deserves it all.*

## Ayah 66: a refusal that is not the Prophet's own opinion

Ibn Kathir gives the ayah in full: *Say: "I have been forbidden to worship those whom you worship besides Allah, since there have come to me evidences from my Lord; and I am commanded to submit to the Lord of all that exists."*

Notice how carefully the sentence is built.

**"Say."** The refusal is not a private conviction kept to himself. He is instructed to state it out loud, to their faces. Ibn Kathir paraphrases it as a direct address: *say, O Muhammad, to these idolators* — that Allah forbids the worship of anyone besides Him, whether these idols or any other false god.

**"I have been forbidden."** The ayah does not have him say *I refuse* or *I have decided against*. It has him say *I have been forbidden* — and, in the second half, *I am commanded*. The messenger stands under the same command he delivers. He is not the author of this religion; he is under orders within it. A prohibition and an order, and he owns neither.

**"Since there have come to me evidences from my Lord."** This is the hinge. He does not refuse their gods out of stubbornness or inherited preference — the very thing he was accusing *them* of. He refuses because clear evidences have reached him. And then, in the ayah that follows, some of those evidences are laid out.

**"And I am commanded to submit to the Lord of all that exists."** The refusal has a positive half. Islam is not merely the demolition of false objects of worship; it is surrender to the true One — and He is named here not as a tribal or local deity but as the Lord of *all that exists*. What is refused is small; what is embraced is everything.

## Ayah 67: the evidence is your own life

Ibn Kathir's comment on the link between the two ayat is the key to the passage: **Allah explains that no one apart from Him is deserving of worship** — and then immediately quotes the creation ayah. Ayah 67 is not a change of subject. It *is* the argument.

The ayah traces a single human life through its stages:

- **from dust** — the origin of the human race
- **then from a Nutfah** — a sperm-drop
- **then from a clot**, which Ibn Kathir's text glosses as *a piece of coagulated blood*
- **then He brings you forth as an infant**
- **then that you may reach the age of full strength**
- **and afterwards to be old**

Ibn Kathir's comment on the whole sequence is a single sentence, and it carries the weight of the argument: *He is the One Who Alone, with no partner or associate, causes you to pass through these different stages, and this happens in accordance with His command, will and decree.*

Sit with the logic of that. Every person hearing this ayah has already been carried through most of these stages. Not one of them chose the moment they were conceived, or supervised their own formation in the womb, or issued the order for their bones to lengthen and their strength to arrive. It happened to them. Something moved them, stage by stage, from dust to a drop to a clot to a crying infant to a strong adult — and whatever that was, it was not the idols, and it was not themselves. Ibn Kathir's phrase "with no partner or associate" is precisely the point at issue: there is no seam anywhere in that process where a second hand could have slipped in.

The repeated **"then"** across the ayah is worth hearing. It marks a sequence — not one act, but stage after stage spread over years. This is not a Creator who wound the world up and walked away. He is the One presently carrying you into the next stage, "in accordance with His command, will and decree."

## "Though some among you die before"

The ayah interrupts its own hopeful arc — infancy, strength, old age — with a sober clause: **"though some among you die before."**

Ibn Kathir explains it with unusual tenderness and precision. It means, he says, dying *before being fully formed and emerging to this world; so his mother miscarries him.* And it means those who *die in infancy or in their youth, or when they are adults but before they reach old age.*

So the list of stages is not a promise. It is a description of the road, and the road is exited at points Allah alone determines. Ibn Kathir supports this by citing another ayah — *that We may make (it) clear to you. And We cause whom We will to remain in the wombs for an appointed term* (22:5) — where even the length of a pregnancy is named as a matter of Allah's will, not a mechanical outcome.

There is quiet comfort here for anyone who has lost a pregnancy or a child. The Qur'an did not overlook them when it listed the ages of a human life. It named them, in the middle of an argument about who deserves worship.

## "That you reach an appointed term, in order that you may understand"

Two purposes close the ayah.

**An appointed term.** The end of your life is not an accident of biology or a statistical average; it is a term already appointed. And notice: the very same phrase, *an appointed term*, was just used in the ayah Ibn Kathir quoted about how long a child remains in the womb. Both ends of the life are fixed by the same hand.

**"In order that you may understand."** The whole sequence is given to you so that you will *think* about it. Ibn Kathir preserves here the reading of **Ibn Jurayj**, who said it means: *"In order that you may remember the Resurrection."*

That is the intended chain of thought, and it is devastatingly simple. You have already watched yourself brought from a drop of fluid to a walking, speaking, reasoning person. You have watched strength arrive and, if you live long enough, you will watch it leave. To reason honestly about that road is to remember where it is going — which is exactly what the next ayah names.

## Ayah 68: life, death, and "Be"

The passage now names the two powers no rival has ever held.

**"It is He Who gives life and causes death."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and absolute: *He is the Only One Who does that, and none is able to do that except He.* Not "He is best at it" — none else can do it at all. And the ayah is built the same way ayah 67 was built, *It is He who…*, so that the two ayat close as a single argument: the One who brought you through the stages is the One who gives life and takes it.

**"And when He decides upon a thing, He says to it only: 'Be!' — and it is."** After a long ayah of stages and intervals, the passage ends in the shortest sentence imaginable: one word of command, one word of compliance, and nothing in between — no effort, no materials, no delay, no resistance. Ibn Kathir explains: *He cannot be opposed or resisted. Whatever He wills definitely comes to pass.*

Place that beside the idols of ayah 66 and the argument closes itself. Whatever they are called and however long they have been honoured, they did not shape you from a drop, they cannot give life, they cannot take it, and no word of theirs makes anything exist. Worship, then, was never a matter of taste. It follows power, and the power is entirely on one side.

## The dignity of the form you were given

Maarif ul Quran pauses on an ayah just before this passage, 40:64 — *and shaped you, and made your shapes so good* — and its reflection illuminates what ayah 67 is quietly claiming.

Allah, it says, blessed the human person with the most distinct, superior and better-balanced form and shape out of all animals. He was given reason. He was given such hands and feet that he could gather materials to make things for his needs and comfort. Even his eating is unlike theirs: animals eat or graze or drink directly with the mouth, and mostly eat single things — some meat, some grass, some leaves. Man uses his hands, and he combines: meat, vegetables, spices, herbs and fruits. He eats by making his food taste good. Maarif ul Quran notes how far this creativity runs — a single fruit taken from nature becomes pies, fruit cakes, jams, preserves and chutneys — and closes with the Qur'an's own words: *Blessed is Allah, the Best Creator.*

The point is not culinary. It is that the very faculties you would use to weigh this argument — reason, hands, the capacity to invent — were themselves handed to you along that same road from dust to full strength. To use the mind He built in order to justify worshipping something else is the strangest ingratitude there is.

## Living it

**Let your own body be your daily proof.** The evidence in this passage is portable. Your ageing, your strength, your childhood photographs, a pregnancy in your family — each is the ayah being read back to you. Ayah 67 ends by asking for exactly this: that you understand from it.

**Refuse clearly, and kindly, as ayah 66 does.** The believer's "no" to false worship is spoken openly, but it is spoken as something he was commanded, not as personal superiority. And it always carries its positive half: not merely *not that*, but submission to the Lord of all that exists.

**Take the appointed term seriously.** Ibn Kathir's list of those who die before old age is a warning against assuming the full sequence is owed to you. The term is already appointed. What remains within your choice is not its length but what fills it.

**Do not fear that what Allah has promised is hard for Him.** The closing words of ayah 68 settle it: He decides, He says *Be*, and it is. In Ibn Kathir's words, He cannot be opposed or resisted, and whatever He wills definitely comes to pass.

passages.title: Disputers of the signs dragged into the Fire
passages.tafsir:
This passage follows a single movement from beginning to end: it starts with a question about people alive right now — those who argue against Allah's signs — and then, without pausing, shows you where that argument ends. Ayah 69 asks how such people can possibly be turned away from the truth; ayat 71–76 answer by drawing back the curtain on the Day of Judgement and letting the reader watch. What holds the unit together is that single thread of consequence: dispute leads to denial, denial leads to chains, chains lead to interrogation, and interrogation ends with the gates of Hell closing on the arrogant.

## The question that opens it (69)

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as Allah addressing His Prophet ﷺ directly: "do you not wonder, O Muhammad, at those who deny the signs of Allah and dispute the truth by means of falsehood, how their minds are diverted from the truth and are misguided?"

Two things in that reading are worth slowing down for.

**"Dispute the truth by means of falsehood."** The problem is not that they have questions. It is that they take up falsehood as a weapon and swing it at something true. The argument is not a search; it is a defence of a position already held.

**"How their minds are diverted."** Notice the shape Ibn Kathir gives the opening: he renders it as an invitation to *wonder* at these people — "do you not wonder, O Muhammad." Their condition is held up as something to marvel at. And his choice of words for what has happened to them is worth sitting with: their minds "are diverted from the truth." Not argued out of it, not reasoned away from it — diverted. It is as though something has taken hold of the compass needle.

## What exactly they denied (70)

Ayah 70 names them: those who denied the Book, and what We sent Our Messengers with. Ibn Kathir explains that second phrase — "that with which We sent Our Messengers" — in four words: **"guidance and clear proof."**

That gloss matters. Notice what is not being rejected. It is not a demand made without evidence, or a claim delivered without argument. What was sent was guidance — a way to walk — and clear proof — a reason to trust the way. To reject that is not neutrality. It is turning down light while standing in the dark.

**"They will come to know."** Ibn Kathir calls this closing phrase "a stern warning and clear threat from the Lord to these people," and links it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Woe that Day to the deniers!" (77:15).

There is a terrible economy in that phrase. It does not describe the punishment; it simply says the knowledge is coming. The dispute in ayah 69 was over what is true. Ayah 70 says: the question will be settled — not by argument, but by arrival. And it is put in the future — *they will* come to know — which is exactly why ayah 71 shifts the camera forward in time to show what that knowing will look like.

## The chains, and the dragging (71–72)

Ayah 71 places iron collars — *al-aghlāl* — around their necks, with chains. Ibn Kathir explains the mechanics: "the chains will be attached to the iron collars, and the keepers of Hell will drag them along on their faces, sometimes to the boiling water, and sometimes to the Fire."

Hold that image against the language of the passage. These were people who *disputed*: articulate, upright, standing on their arguments. Now the neck is collared and the body is dragged, face down, with no say in the direction of travel. The one thing they will not be doing is arguing.

Ibn Kathir gathers a set of parallel passages to fill in the scene — "This is the Hell which the criminals denied. They will go between it and the fierce boiling water!" (55:43–44); the tree of Zaqqūm (which Ibn Kathir describes as a bitter tree of Hell) eaten until bellies are filled, then boiling water drunk on top of it "like thirsty camels" (56:41–44, 51–56); and the passage in Sūrah al-Dukhān where the command comes, "Seize him and drag him into the midst of blazing Fire, then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. Taste you (this)! Verily, you were (pretending to be) the mighty, the generous!" (44:43–50). Ibn Kathir adds a note about that last line: it is said to them "to rebuke and ridicule them." The titles they carried in the world — mighty, generous — are read back to them as mockery.

**A word on al-ḥamīm.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on ayah 72 and takes up a real puzzle. *Al-ḥamīm* means boiling hot water. The wording of 71–72 — dragged *into the ḥamīm*, then thrown into the Fire as fuel — seems to place the boiling water somewhere before the Fire, and therefore perhaps outside Jahannam altogether. The verse "Then, their return is but to the Fire" (37:68) points the same way: they are brought to the ḥamīm to drink its water, and are then returned to Jahannam. But other verses put the ḥamīm inside: "This is the Jahannam that the guilty people deny. They will circle around between it and between hot, boiling water" (55:43–44).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves it without forcing either text: "there is no contradiction between these two things. There will be many strata or sections of Jahannam itself serving as venues of many kinds of punishment." The ḥamīm is one such section. Because it has its own separate and distinct location it can be called outside; because it is still a section of Jahannam itself, it can also be called Jahannam. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir's reading fits this exactly — the people of Jahannam, shackled in chains, will sometimes be dragged into the ḥamīm and at other times into Jahannam.

This is worth noticing as a method as much as a conclusion. Two verses appear to pull in opposite directions; the commentator does not discard one, and does not flatten either into metaphor. He lets both stand and finds the picture large enough to hold them.

## The interrogation (73–74)

Then the questioning begins. Ayah 73: "Where are those you used to associate as partners besides Allah?" Ibn Kathir renders the force of it plainly: "where are the idols whom you used to worship instead of Allah? Can they help you today?"

This is the moment when the whole structure of *shirk* — setting up partners alongside Allah and directing worship to them — is tested. It collapses twice over.

**First collapse: absence.** They answer, "They have vanished from us." Ibn Kathir: "they have gone away and they cannot do anything for us." Every claim ever made for those partners was a claim about help. At the one moment when help is the only thing that matters, they are simply not there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a sharp detail. The disbelievers say the idols are "lost to us" in the sense that they do not see them around — "though, they might as well be lying somewhere in a corner of Jahannam," since other verses establish that what was worshipped besides Allah is itself in the Fire: "Surely, you and whatever you worship other than Allah are the fuel for Jahannam" (21:98). So the worshipped are not necessarily elsewhere. They may be in the same place, unseen and unable to do a thing for anyone.

**Second collapse: denial.** Then comes the stranger half of ayah 74 — "Nay, we did not call upon anything before." Ibn Kathir explains: "they will deny that they worshipped them," and cites the parallel in Sūrah al-Anʿām: "There will then be (left) no Fitnah (excuse) for them but to say: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah'" (6:23). (*Fitnah* here is glossed in the citation itself as "excuse" — there will be nothing left for them to fall back on but this denial.)

Think about what has just happened. In the presence of Allah, in the Fire, with the truth entirely unavoidable, the reflex is still to lie. The habit of disputing falsehood against truth — the very thing ayah 69 opened with — has not died with the world. It follows them in. That is perhaps the most sobering line in the passage: a person can lose everything and still not lose the argument-reflex that ruined him.

**"Thus Allah leads astray the disbelievers."** The passage seals this scene with those words. We affirm it as Allah has said it, without explaining it away. And note how the passage itself frames the justice of it: ayah 69 asks how they turned away, ayah 70 records that they denied guidance and clear proof that had reached them, and ayah 75 states outright that what they suffer is "because" of what they did. Misguidance is in Allah's hand; the passage insists in the same breath that it fell on people who had been given light and turned from it.

## Why: faraḥ and maraḥ (75)

Ayah 75 gives the reason: "That was because you had been exulting in the earth without any right, and that you used to rejoice extremely." Ibn Kathir notes that this is spoken by the angels — "what you are suffering now is your recompense for your exulting in the earth without any right, and for your extravagance."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two Arabic verbs here, and this is the passage's richest piece of language work.

**Tafraḥūn** comes from *faraḥ*, which simply means to be happy. **Tamraḥūn** comes from *maraḥ*, which means "to exult unduly or to trample over the rights of others by priding on one's wealth and power." That kind of undue exultation, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is "absolutely blameworthy and Haram (unlawful)" — *ḥarām* meaning forbidden.

Now look at the wording of the ayah, because a great deal hangs on it. *Faraḥ* is **qualified**: it is condemned *bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq* — "wrongfully," without any right. *Maraḥ* carries **no such qualifier**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion directly: *maraḥ* "is a cause of punishment absolutely, without any restriction. Therefore, no qualifying words were added to it." But joy needed the qualifier, because not all joy is blameworthy.

So there are two degrees of *faraḥ*:

- **The forbidden kind** — "seeking enjoyment out of sinfulness under the intoxication of wealth coupled with the absence of any thought of there being a Lord over them." This is what the ayah means, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, pointing to the same word used against Qārūn: "Do not exult. Surely, Allah does not like the exultant" (28:76).
- **The praiseworthy kind** — "that one takes good things of life as blessings from Allah Taʿālā, and expresses his or her joy on having these." This is not merely allowed; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it permissible, in fact *mustaḥabb* (recommended) and desirable, citing "with these they should rejoice" (10:58).

The distinction is not in the amount of pleasure but in what the pleasure is attached to. Being pleased with rightful, permissible blessings as an expression of gratitude is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, "an act of ʿibādah (worship of Allah) and thawāb (reward from Him)." Jubilating over what is undue and impermissible is what is being paid for in ayah 75.

This should land as relief as well as warning. This passage is not saying that enjoying your life is dangerous. It is saying that pleasure taken in sin, with Allah edited out of the picture, is dangerous — and that trampling on the rights of others out of pride in wealth and power is condemned with no qualifier and no exception.

## The gates close (76)

The passage ends with a command: "Enter the gates of Hell to abide therein" — and then the verdict, "what an evil abode of the arrogant." Ibn Kathir: "what a terrible abode and final destination, filled with humiliation and severe punishment for those who arrogantly ignored the signs of Allah and refused to accept His proof and evidence."

Notice that the final word of the passage names the root disease. Not "the deniers," not "the disputers" — *al-mutakabbirīn*, the arrogant. Ayah 69 described the behaviour; ayah 76 names what was underneath it all along. And Ibn Kathir joins the two together in one line: these are people who "arrogantly ignored the signs of Allah and refused to accept His proof and evidence." Someone in that position is not, at bottom, unconvinced. He is unwilling.

There is a bitter symmetry in the geography too. The arrogant carry themselves in the world as though every door is theirs to walk through. The last door they walk through is one they are ordered into.

## Living it

The passage is a warning, but it hands the ordinary believer some very concrete things.

**Watch the reflex to argue.** Ayah 69 condemns disputing truth by means of falsehood, and ayah 74 shows that reflex still firing in the Fire. The safeguard is a habit built now: when evidence goes against you, examine it rather than defend yourself.

**Test what you lean on.** Ayah 73 is a question you can ask yourself while it can still be answered without loss: what am I actually depending on, and will it be there on that Day? Whatever answers "no" is, to that extent, in the same category as the partners that vanished.

**Keep your joy attached.** Enjoy the good things — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic that joy in rightful blessings, expressed as gratitude, is recommended and rewarded, and is itself an act of worship. Delight taken in what is impermissible, with no thought of Allah, or exultation that tramples the rights of others, is what ayah 75 collects the debt for.

**Take arrogance as seriously as the ayah does.** Since ayah 76 makes arrogance the defining trait of that abode, humility before Allah's revelation is not a soft virtue at the edge of religion. It is the thing that decides which side of the gate a person stands on.

And Allah knows best.

passages.title: Be patient: the promise and the decree to come
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are Allah's word of steadying to His Messenger ﷺ as the sūrah draws toward its close: hold firm, because what has been promised is not in doubt — only its timing is. Ayah 77 gives the command and the certainty; ayah 78 widens the frame, placing the Prophet ﷺ in a long line of messengers who waited on Allah's leave rather than on their own timetable. What holds the passage together is a single idea: **the outcome is settled, the schedule is not yours, and patience is what stands between the two.**

## "So be patient" — a command given to a man who was waiting

After all that has passed in the sūrah, the address turns directly to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir puts the sense of the command plainly: here Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ **to patiently bear the rejection of those who rejected him**, and behind the command is a promise — that he would be victorious and would prevail over his people, and that he and those who followed him would be the successful ones in this world and the Hereafter.

Notice what kind of patience is being asked for. It is not the patience of someone who has been told nothing. It is the patience of someone who has been told everything except *when*. The clause that follows the command — **"Surely Allah's promise is true"** — is the reason attached to the command, not a separate thought. You are asked to be patient precisely *because* the thing you are waiting for is guaranteed. Patience here is not resignation to an unknown outcome; it is composure in front of a known one.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out something tender in this. Reading the verse, it observes that **the Holy Prophet ﷺ was hopefully waiting for the disbelievers to be punished** — and that it was precisely to comfort him that he was asked to be somewhat patient about it. The command is consolation shaped as instruction. Allah does not rebuke that longing. He confirms the promise behind it and asks for a little more waiting.

## The two branches of ayah 77 — and both end in the same place

The verse then splits the future into two possibilities, and this is the heart of its comfort:

> "Whether We show you some part of what We have promised them, **or** We cause you to die, then still it is to Us they all shall be returned."

Two roads, one destination. Either the Prophet ﷺ lives to see a portion of it — note that the wording says **some part** of what was promised, not all of it — or he is taken before it arrives. Either way, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises, the promise of Allah that they will be punished **will certainly be fulfilled: it may be during his lifetime, or after he has departed from the mortal world.** The one thing that is *not* on the table is that it fails to happen.

**The first branch was fulfilled in his lifetime.** Ibn Kathir reads "We show you some part of what We have promised them" as referring to this world, and says simply: *this is what happened.* Allah gave them the joy of humiliating the leaders and nobles of the Quraysh, who were killed on the day of Badr. Then Allah granted them victory over Makkah and over the entire Arabian Peninsula, during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. So the very figures who had led the rejection were the ones brought low, and the promise moved from words into events within his own lifetime.

**The second branch loses nothing.** On "or We cause you to die, then still it is to Us they all shall be returned," Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as: *and We shall inflict a severe punishment upon them in the Hereafter.* Death does not close the file. The return to Allah is not an escape route for the wrongdoer; it is the transfer of the case to the only court that cannot be evaded. So a delay that looks like reprieve is only a change of venue.

This is why the verse relieves anxiety rather than merely postponing it. The Prophet's ﷺ witnessing the outcome is a mercy granted to him; the verse makes clear it was never a condition of the outcome arriving.

## Is waiting for punishment compatible with being a mercy to the worlds?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection honestly, and it is worth sitting with, because a thoughtful reader feels it too. Waiting for the disbelievers to be punished **apparently seems contrary to the dignity of one who was sent with universal mercy.** How does the Prophet of mercy hope for a punishment to fall?

The answer given is precise: **here the matter is different.** When the purpose of punishing criminals is to bring comfort to innocent believers who were oppressed, then the punishment of criminals is not contrary to compassion and mercy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point with an appeal to ordinary moral sense: **nobody regards the punishment given to a criminal as against the dictate of mercy.**

So the longing is not in tension with mercy once you see what it is aimed at — the relief of people who were wronged. And even so, notice that Allah still tells him to be patient. Even a longing that is legitimate is placed under Allah's timing rather than the servant's.

## Ayah 78: "We already sent messengers before you"

Ibn Kathir marks the transition explicitly — after the promise of ayah 77, **Allah says, consoling His Prophet ﷺ** — and then comes the wider horizon of ayah 78. The consolation works by placing him in company.

**"Of some of them We have related to you their story."** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah says the like of this in Sūrat An-Nisāʾ, and gives the sense: *We have revealed the stories of some of them and how their people disbelieved in them, but the Messengers ultimately prevailed.* That last phrase is the whole point of telling the stories at all. The pattern the Prophet ﷺ was living through — a truthful man, a rejecting people, a long stretch of apparent stalemate — is not an anomaly and not a sign of failure. It is the shape the earlier missions took, and its ending, in those accounts, is that the messengers prevail. So the earlier narratives running through the Qur'an are not decoration; they are evidence submitted on the Prophet's ﷺ behalf.

**"And of some We have not related to you their story."** Ibn Kathir says of these that they are **many, many more than those whose stories have been told** — again referencing what is stated in Sūrat An-Nisāʾ — and he pauses at the thought to say: *praise and blessings be to Allah.* There is a quiet humbling here. Behind the handful of names we know stands a vast company of Allah's messengers whose stories were not related to us, and whose struggles are known to Him. If you have ever felt that your effort for Allah is unseen, this half-verse is worth holding: being unnarrated to humanity is not the same as being unknown to Allah.

## "No messenger could bring a sign except by Allah's leave"

The ayah then turns to the matter of signs — the miracles by which a messenger's truthfulness was made evident. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning of the clause directly: **none of the Prophets was able to bring miracles to his people except when Allah granted him permission to do that**, as a sign of the truth of the message he brought them.

This settles two things at once. First, it settles who is in charge. A messenger is a messenger, not a proprietor of the unseen. Miracles are not at his own disposal; they are granted by Allah's leave, when He wills, for the purpose Ibn Kathir names — to authenticate the message he brought. So the absence of a sign at any given moment reflects Allah's decision, not a shortfall in the messenger.

Second, it deepens the patience command of ayah 77. If even the signs are on Allah's schedule, then of course the promised reckoning is too. The messenger's task is delivery and steadfastness; permission, timing, and outcome belong to Allah. That is a liberating division of labour, and it is the reason the Prophet ﷺ could be told simply, *be patient.*

## "When the command of Allah comes, the matter is decided with truth"

The passage closes with the moment the waiting ends. Ibn Kathir reads **"when comes the commandment of Allah"** as meaning His punishment and vengeance which will encompass the disbelievers — the decisive intervention, whenever Allah brings it.

And then: **"the matter will be decided with truth."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is two-sided, and both sides matter — **the believers will be saved and the disbelievers will be destroyed.** A decision "with truth" is not merely a verdict of condemnation; it is rescue and ruin in one event, seen from two positions.

The last phrase names the losers by what they had attached themselves to: **"and the followers of falsehood will then be lost."** Not by tribe, wealth or standing — by allegiance. And note the word *then*: the loss registers at that moment, when the command arrives. Until then, falsehood may look like it is doing well. The verse does not say it becomes worthless at that point; it says that is when its bearers are shown to be the losers.

## Living it

**Patience is the response to certainty, not to doubt.** The command in ayah 77 comes attached to its reason — Allah's promise is true. So when you are asked to endure something, the question to hold on to is not "will this ever be put right?" but "am I willing to leave the timing to Allah?"

**You may not see the outcome, and that is allowed.** The Prophet ﷺ himself was told he might be taken before the promise landed. If Allah's own Messenger was asked to accept that, then working faithfully at something whose vindication you never witness is not a failed life — it is the pattern.

**Delay is not denial.** "Then still it is to Us they all shall be returned" — and Ibn Kathir's reading of it is a severe punishment in the Hereafter. Every unpunished wrong is on file, not dismissed. This should cool the urge to force outcomes ourselves, and it should also frighten us into examining our own file.

**You are not alone in the pattern.** Ayah 78 exists to console the Prophet ﷺ under the rejection he was facing, by telling him that messengers went before him, that their people disbelieved in them, and that they ultimately prevailed. Feeling out of step with your surroundings for the sake of the truth is not evidence you are wrong.

**Don't demand signs; do the work.** No messenger brought a sign except by Allah's leave. Neither the proof nor the timing was ever in the messenger's hands — only the faithfulness. That is all that is being asked of us either.

passages.title: Cattle and ships among His signs
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After a long stretch of warning, argument and the promise that Allah's word will come to pass, the surah turns the reader's eyes to something utterly ordinary: livestock, and ships. Three ayat, one movement — ayah 79 and ayah 80 lay out the gift, and ayah 81 turns it into a question the listener cannot escape: *"And He shows you His signs. Now which of Allah's signs will you deny?"* Ibn Kathir titles this section exactly that way: **"The Cattle are also a Blessing from Allah and a Sign from Him."** A blessing and a proof, in the same creature.

## Where we are in the surah

Just before this, in ayah 77, the Prophet ﷺ was told: *"Therefore, be patient. Surely, the promise of Allah is true. Then, whether We show you [in your life] a part of the promise We are making to them, or make you die [before they are punished], in any case they have to be returned to Us."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as telling us something about the Prophet's ﷺ state: from this verse it appears he was hopefully waiting for the disbelievers to be punished, and the ayah comes to comfort him — the promise will certainly be fulfilled, whether during his lifetime or after he has departed from this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then raises the objection a sensitive reader might feel: waiting for disbelievers to be punished *apparently* seems contrary to the dignity of one sent with universal mercy. Its answer is that here the matter is different. When the purpose of punishing criminals is to bring comfort to innocent believers who were oppressed, the punishment of criminals is not contrary to compassion and mercy. Nobody regards the punishment given to a criminal as against the dictate of mercy.

Hold that beside our three ayat, and the tone of the closing question comes into focus. Before any punishment is mentioned, Allah points at the livestock and the ships and asks what, exactly, is to be denied.

## Ayah 79 — "Allah, it is He Who has made cattle for you"

The ayah, in Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"Allah, it is He Who has made cattle for you, that you may ride on some of them, and of some you eat."*

**The word.** The Arabic is *al-anʿām*. Ibn Kathir spells out its reference: **camels, cows and sheep**. And he notes the division the ayah itself makes — *some of them they ride and some of them they eat*. The provision is not one undifferentiated thing; it is sorted, some for carrying, some for the table.

**Ibn Kathir's inventory.** He then takes the three animals one at a time, and it is worth following him slowly, because the point is accumulation:

- **Camels** — they may be ridden or eaten; their milk is drunk; and they are used for carrying heavy burdens on journeys to distant lands.
- **Cattle** — they are eaten and their milk is drunk; and they are used for plowing the earth.
- **Sheep** — they are eaten and their milk is also drunk.

And then, cutting across all three: *the hair and wool of all of these animals is used to make tents, clothing and furnishings.* Ibn Kathir adds that this has already been discussed in Surat al-Anʿām and Surat an-Nahl.

Notice what that list amounts to. Transport, meat, milk, farming, shelter, clothing, the furnishings of a home. Take these animals away and you have removed travel, food, agriculture and roof at once. This, says Ibn Kathir, is Allah **reminding His servants of His blessing** in that He created the cattle for them.

## Ayah 80 — benefits, a desire in the breast, and ships

*"And you have (many other) benefits from them, and that you may reach by their means a desire that is in your breasts, and on them and on ships you are carried."*

The ayah widens the frame in three steps.

**"And you have (many other) benefits from them."** Riding and eating have already been named. Now the ayah adds *manāfiʿ* — benefits — without listing them. Ibn Kathir's inventory above gives us some of what fills that space: milk, wool, hair, ploughing, the carrying of heavy loads.

**"That you may reach by their means a desire that is in your breasts."** A desire *in the breast* — the ayah does not describe the journey in terms of ground covered but in terms of something wanted. Ibn Kathir's note on the camel sits beside it: they are used for carrying heavy burdens on journeys to distant lands.

**"And on them and on ships you are carried."** In one phrase the ayah joins the animals to the ships, land travel to sea travel. And note the wording: not "you ride," not "you sail," but *you are carried* — the human being appears here as the one being borne along by what Allah made.

## Ayah 81 — "which of Allah's signs will you deny?"

**"And He shows you His Ayat."** Ibn Kathir glosses *āyāt* here as **"His proof and evidence, on the horizons and in yourselves."** A sign, in this reading, is not decoration. It is testimony — something that argues.

Two locations, then. Outward, *on the horizons*: the herd, the sea, the ship carrying its load of people. Inward, *in yourselves*: Ibn Kathir does not spell out the inward evidence here, though the ayah just before has already pointed inside — *a desire that is in your breasts*.

**"Which, then, of the Ayat of Allah do you deny?"** Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt: this means **you cannot deny any of His signs and proofs, unless you are stubborn and arrogant.**

That is a precise diagnosis, and it is the heart of the passage. On this reading, denial is not a failure of information. The evidence is not obscure, not distant, not reserved for scholars — it is the animal that feeds you and the vessel that carries you. So when a person still refuses, Ibn Kathir locates the problem not in what they know but in what they are: stubbornness and arrogance. This is why the passage sits where it does, just after the promise of ayah 77 that the deniers will be dealt with. They were not short of proof.

## Living it

**Re-read your ordinary day as evidence.** The passage's method is not to send you looking for a miracle. It takes the plainest furniture of life — food, milk, wool, transport, shelter — and calls it *āyāt*, proof. Ibn Kathir's phrase "on the horizons and in yourselves" reads like a standing instruction: the material is already around you and already in you.

**Notice the wording: "you are carried."** Whatever carries you today stands where the animals and the ships stand in ayah 80 — something you did not make, doing the work of getting you there.

**Gratitude is the honest response to a sign.** Ayah 79 opens with *Allah, it is He Who* — the Giver is named before a single use is listed. Ibn Kathir reads the whole passage as Allah reminding His servants of His blessing; to take the benefits and forget the Source is precisely the posture the closing question comes to break.

**Take the question personally.** *Which of Allah's signs will you deny?* It was aimed at those who rejected outright, and Ibn Kathir tells us plainly what such rejection requires: stubbornness and arrogance. But the question will still search a believer — not "do you deny the signs?" but: which of them do you live as though they were nothing?

passages.title: Faith that comes too late to save
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Surah Ghafir with a warning drawn from history: nation after nation was offered guidance, preferred its own knowledge, and only believed when the punishment was already in front of its eyes — at which point belief was worth nothing. What holds ayat 82–85 together is a single unbroken sequence: the ruins are still there (82), here is why those people fell (83), here is what they said at the last moment (84), and here is why it did not save them (85).

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a line back to ayah 77, where the Prophet ﷺ was told: *"Therefore, be patient. Surely, the promise of Allah is true. Then, whether We show you [in your life] a part of the promise We are making to them, or make you die [before they are punished], in any case they have to be returned to Us."* From that verse, the commentary observes, it appears the Prophet ﷺ was hopefully waiting for the disbelievers to be punished, and so — to comfort him — he was asked to be somewhat patient about it: Allah's promise that they will be punished will certainly be fulfilled, whether during his lifetime or after he has departed from this mortal world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then pauses over an objection a thoughtful reader might feel — waiting for the disbelievers to be punished apparently seems contrary to the dignity of one sent with universal mercy. Its answer: here the matter is different. When the purpose of punishing criminals is to bring comfort to innocent believers who were oppressed, the punishment of those criminals is not contrary to compassion and mercy. Nobody regards the punishment given to a criminal as against the dictate of mercy. That framing matters for reading ayat 82–85. This is not gloating over ruins; it is the vindication of the wronged, and a last warning to those still able to heed it.

## Ayah 82 — the argument written into the landscape

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: *"Have they not traveled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? They were more in number than them and mightier in strength, and in the traces in the land; yet all that they used to earn availed them not."*

The Arabic word rendered here as "the end" is **ʿāqibah**. What a nation finally came to is not, in this ayah, a matter of rumour or report: it is a place you can walk through.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us about the nations who rejected their Messengers in ancient times, and he mentions the severe punishment they suffered **despite** their great strength. The ayah itself stacks the comparison: they were **more in number**, **mightier in strength**, and greater in the **traces** they left in the land. Ibn Kathir mentions the traces they left behind in the earth and the great wealth they amassed. And then the verdict: *"yet all that they used to earn availed them not."*

Notice what the ayah does with a people's assets. Population, military power, monumental building, accumulated earnings — these are precisely the things a society counts as insurance against catastrophe. The ayah does not deny that they had them in greater measure than those being warned. It denies that any of it *worked*. As Ibn Kathir puts it, none of that availed them anything and could not prevent the punishment of Allah at all. The invitation to travel through the earth is therefore an invitation to walk past the strongest possible counter-evidence to your own sense of security and see it lying in pieces.

## Ayah 83 — the knowledge that flattered them to death

Ayah 83 gives the diagnosis. Ibn Kathir renders it: *"Then when their Messengers came to them with clear proofs, they were glad (and proud) with that which they had of the knowledge (of worldly things). And that at which they used to mock, surrounded them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same clause: *"they exulted because of whatever of knowledge they had."*

Hold those renderings side by side — "glad (and proud)," "exulted," and As-Suddi's "they rejoiced." This was not mere disagreement with the Messengers; they were *pleased with themselves* while disagreeing. Ibn Kathir writes that when the Messengers came to them with clear signs and decisive evidence, they did not pay any attention to them; instead they were content with the knowledge with them — or so they claimed — and said that they did not need what the Messengers brought them.

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites sharpen this:

- **Mujahid** said: "They said, we know better than them, we will not be resurrected and we will not be punished."
- **As-Suddi** said: "In their ignorance, they rejoiced in what they had of (worldly) knowledge. So Allah sent upon them a punishment which they could not escape or resist."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the obvious question directly: what was this knowledge, with which the disbelievers were exultant to the extent that they would even reject the body of knowledge brought by prophets? It offers two possibilities.

**First**, it could be some sort of **al-jahl al-murakkab** — "compounded ignorance," which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains as the state of an ignorant person who, despite his sheer ignorance, believes himself to be knowledgeable. The commentary notes bluntly that this does not qualify to be "knowledge" at all.

**Second**, it may mean genuine competence — awareness in the fields of trade, industry and things like that. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grants that they really had expertise in these fields according to their time. This is the more sobering reading, because the knowledge is real; it is simply the wrong instrument for the question in front of them. The commentary connects it to Surah ar-Rum: *"They know something superficial of the worldly life, but of the Hereafter they are negligent"* (30:7). Such people, it says, do know a good deal about the material life of the world and how to get most benefited by it, but are totally ignorant or heedless of the Hereafter — where they have to live forever, either in bliss or in bane, both of them everlasting.

Even on that second reading, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazharī) draws the same conclusion: since these people deny the Day of Judgment and the Hereafter and do not know — or do not *want* to know — its everlasting reward and punishment, they do not see anything beyond their knowledge of the apparent, are quite pleased with it, and as a result do not pay heed to the areas of knowledge brought by the noble prophets.

**And what they laughed at closed in on them.** The ayah ends: *"And that at which they used to mock, surrounded them."* Ibn Kathir glosses **ḥāqa bihim** — "and surrounded them" — as meaning "encompassed them," and glosses *"that at which they used to mock"* as that which they used to disbelieve in and said would never happen. There is a terrible symmetry here: the very thing they had treated as a joke became the wall around them. Mockery is not a refutation. What you laugh at does not go away; it waits.

## Ayah 84 — the right words at the wrong hour

Ibn Kathir renders it: *"So when they saw Our punishment, they said: 'We believe in Allah Alone and reject (all) that we used to associate with Him as (His) partners.'"*

Read the words themselves: this is a flawless declaration. Ibn Kathir says they affirmed that Allah is One and denied the false gods. That is tawḥīd stated and shirk renounced — affirmation and negation together, exactly what had been asked of them from the first day. Nothing is wrong with the content. Everything is wrong with the timing. Ibn Kathir's phrase is precise: this was at the time when excuses were to no avail.

Note also the trigger in the wording of the ayah: *"when they **saw** Our punishment"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning when they saw with their own eyes the punishment which came upon them. Their faith was not a response to evidence weighed and reflected upon; it was pulled out of them by the sight of the thing itself. Faith produced under those conditions is barely a choice at all, and the whole test of this life is that it be a choice made while the unseen is still unseen.

Ibn Kathir gives the archetypal case: Firʿawn, as he was drowning, said, *"I believe that none has the right to be worshipped but He in Whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am one of the Muslims"* (10:90). But Allah said: *"Now (you believe) while you refused to believe before and you were one of the corrupters"* (10:91). Ibn Kathir explains that Allah did not accept this from him, because He had answered the prayer of His Prophet Musa (peace be upon him), when he said, *"And harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment"* (10:88).

## Ayah 85 — a law, not an exception

Ibn Kathir renders it: *"Then their Faith could not avail them when they saw Our punishment. (Like) this has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants. And there the disbelievers lost utterly."*

The clause that turns a story into a principle is **sunnat Allāh allatī qad khalat fī ʿibādihi** — rendered above as *"(Like) this has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants."* Ibn Kathir states its force as a ruling: this is the ruling of Allah concerning **all** those who repent only when they actually see the punishment — He does not accept that from them. So what happened to those earlier nations, and to Firʿawn, is not a series of one-off severities. It is one settled way of dealing, applied again and again. That is why ayah 82 sent us out to travel the earth: the ruins are the case record, and they are consistent.

And so the closing words on them: *"And there the disbelievers lost utterly."*

## The door that closes — and how long it stays open

Ibn Kathir brings this principle down from the level of destroyed nations to the level of one dying person, which is where it touches us. He introduces it with the words "It says in the Hadith," and reports that Allah will accept the repentance of His servant **so long as the death rattle is not sounding in his throat**. (The commentary before us does not name the collection in which this hadith is recorded, so we relate the teaching as Ibn Kathir relates it, without attaching a source we cannot verify. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the same hadith — "Allah accepts the taubah [repentance] of the servant before the agony and rattle of death overtakes him" — and attributes it to Ibn Kathir.)

Once the death rattle is sounding, Ibn Kathir explains, and the soul has reached the throat, and the dying person actually *sees* the angel of death — then he can no longer repent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān joins the two halves together: it is after seeing the punishment that these people confess to the true faith, but a declaration of faith at this late hour is not acceptable and trustworthy with Allah; similarly, once divine punishment has come face to face, no repentance and no declaration of faith made by anyone remains acceptable.

Put together, both halves of the message stand — and the merciful half is far the larger:

- **The door is astonishingly wide.** Repentance is accepted right up to the point where the death rattle begins. Ibn Kathir's citation places the deadline at that last moment, not at some earlier point of no return.
- **The door does close.** And it closes at a moment nobody gets to schedule. The people of ayah 84 were not refused because their words were wrong; they were refused because they had waited until the punishment was in front of their eyes. When the unseen becomes seen, believing in it is no longer faith.

## Living it

**Do not let competence stand in for guidance.** The people of ayah 83 were not fools in worldly terms; on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's second reading they really had expertise in trade and industry according to their time. Their error was treating knowledge of the apparent as though it settled questions about the Hereafter. Skill in your field tells you nothing about your ʿāqibah.

**Watch for delight in your own opinion.** They were *glad and proud* with what they had. That self-satisfaction is what stopped them paying attention to clear signs and decisive evidence. The remedy for compounded ignorance is not more information; it is the humility to suspect that what you are most certain of may be exactly where you are blind.

**Take mockery seriously as a symptom.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is that what they mocked was what they disbelieved in and said would never happen. When a reality is unwelcome, laughing at it is the cheapest way to avoid weighing it — and it changes nothing about whether that reality arrives.

**Repent now, while it is still repentance.** The most practical implication of ayah 85 is that turning back is worth most precisely when nothing is forcing you to. Faith offered while the outcome is still hidden is the faith that the way of Allah accepts.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes its commentary on this surah with a supplication that gathers all of this into a few words — worth learning by heart:

> O Allah, we ask of You the obliteration of all sins, and well-being, and repentance **before** death, and ease and pardon **at the time of** death, and forgiveness and mercy **after** death, with the barakah of Al Ha Meem, and blessings of Allah on the noble prophet ﷺ.

With these ayat the tafsir of Surah Ghafir comes to an end. Ibn Kathir signs off simply: praise and thanks be to Allah.
